#4596. Tesla confirms Vietnam entry to take on VinFast and its 36% market share

Tesla has started hiring in Vietnam, and one of its recruiters says the company is now “officially coming” to the country. The five open roles include a sales manager, a service manager, and a charging project developer.

It’s a tough market to walk into. VinFast, the local all-electric automaker, has sold roughly 36% of every new car in Vietnam this year, more than its next five competitors combined.

Tesla quietly registered Tesla Motors Vietnam LLC in Ho Chi Minh City on September 11, with about 77.7 billion dong (roughly $3 million) in charter capital and a business scope covering car imports, wholesale, and retail. Tesla never commented on it.

Now we have the first confirmation from someone inside the company. Ricky Ip, who recruits for Tesla, posted on X this morning:

Tesla is officially coming to Vietnam – and we're hiring.Our mission is to build a world of amazing abundance and we are looking for passionate people to join us in Vietnam and help make that vision a reality. Current Job Openings:Sales Manager – https://t.co/AvW3higssS… pic.twitter.com/YDZvLNmz8P

The five openings are Sales Manager, Service Manager, HR Business Partner, Purchasing Manager, and Project Developer, Charging. That last one is the tell. You don’t hire someone to develop charging projects unless you plan to build Superchargers in the country.

Tesla has followed this playbook before in Southeast Asia. It went on a hiring spree in Thailand in September 2022 and opened orders there three months later. It started hiring in the Philippines in September 2024 and launched in early 2025. So a Vietnam launch in the next few months wouldn’t be a surprise.

There’s no word yet on pricing, models, or store locations. Oddly, the recruiting graphic features the next-generation Roadster, with fine print saying the vehicle is “for illustration purposes only.” Fair enough.

Tesla isn’t walking into an empty market. It’s walking into VinFast’s backyard.

VinFast delivered 177,697 cars in Vietnam through the first nine months of 2026, out of a national total of about 495,000. That’s about 36% of the entire car market, gas cars included. In September alone, it had 37.7% of the market.

Here’s how the year-to-date numbers stack up against the next brands:

Add up Toyota, Hyundai, Mitsubishi, Ford, and Kia and you get 175,136. VinFast alone beat all five of them.

And it’s already passed its full-year 2025 volume with a quarter left to go. VinFast says September was its 25th straight month as Vietnam’s best-selling car brand.

The model mix tells you a lot about the market. The VinFast VF 3, a tiny two-door electric crossover that launched at under $13,000, is Vietnam’s best-selling vehicle so far this year. VinFast models held the top five spots in September.

VinFast builds its cars in Haiphong. Tesla would have to import everything, most likely from Giga Shanghai, and Vietnam kept passenger cars on its high-tariff list under the ASEAN-China free trade agreement.

Expanding to Vietnam is a logical step considering the other markets nearby that Tesla is already selling in. In these markets, a smaller and affordable car (model 2) would have been a big seller.

Charging is another gap. VinFast’s sister company V-Green runs the country’s dominant charging network and announced plans this year to spend about $380 million on 99 ultra-fast charging stations. Third-party networks in Vietnam are still thin.

There is one thing working in Tesla’s favor. Vietnam just extended its registration fee exemption for battery-electric cars through the end of 2030, and that applies to imported EVs too.

And VinFast’s volume comes with an asterisk. A significant share of its deliveries go to GSM, the Xanh SM electric taxi and ride-hailing company founded by VinFast chairman Pham Nhat Vuong. VinFast has long relied on Vietnam for the bulk of its deliveries, which we pointed out when it delivered nearly 100,000 EVs in 2024.

#4595. How to Be Happy for the Rest of Your Life

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 7, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

You wake up in the morning, a little achier than you were the day before. Maybe you overdid it at the gym, or it’s raining, and you can feel it in your joints. Without giving it a second’s thought, you conclude that the aging process is rearing its ugly head once again.

It might surprise you to find out, or maybe you know it already, that the majority of older adults actually are pretty satisfied with their lives, even if things aren’t ideal. Researchers attribute the “paradox of well-being” to the ability that the average person in later life has to focus on the positive and set aside whatever objective disappointments may happen on any given day.

What are some of the secrets to becoming one of these lucky people? New research on aging and happiness provides some intriguing answers.

You can probably relate to the idea that feeling in control of your fate can help you get through difficult times. Aging may not feel as if it is something you can control. But what if it is?

According to new research by Friedrich Schiller University Jena’s Maria Wirth and colleagues (2026), we all perform a lifelong balancing act between perceived age-related gains and losses. Happiness, they go on to propose, is the outcome of making an assessment on the gains side. When you perceive age-related gains, this becomes both conducive to happiness and facilitates your adaptation by helping you appreciate your life experiences more fully. If losses dominate your psychological horizon, you’ll feel demoralized and hopeless.

The trick to swinging the balance to the positive side rests, the authors propose, on your ability to employ self-regulatory strategies. Translated into the concept of perceived control, this means that you feel your actions can bring about desired outcomes. Sure, your knees may ache, but engaging your sense of control means you think that, by a combination of stretching and yoga (two excellent strategies), you’ll come out okay.

Using a daily diary study, Wirth and team pinged their sample of 268 older adults (average age 65) daily for two weeks with questionnaires assessing their overall gains-losses ratio, sense of personal control, and happiness. The personal control measure asked participants to rate on a 4-point agree-disagree scale such as, “In the past 24 hours, I had quite a bit of influence on the degree to which I could be involved in activities.” Because the data tracked people over time, the role of control in predicting happiness could be compared across and within individuals.

Starting with the across-person analyses, the results showed that the happiness-losses relationship went in the predicted negative direction for people low in control; feeling that your losses outweighed your gains would lead you to feel more unhappy, but only if you perceived these losses as outside your control.

The findings showed that a lower sense of age-related gains was more detrimental to an individual’s happiness on days the person felt a lower-than-average degree of control.

Overall, as the authors concluded, control was the #1 influence on how perceived gains and losses predicted happiness. If you feel in control, your gains or losses on any given day won’t upset your equilibrium. Only when your control seems to have slipped away will the perceived losses get you down.

A sense of personal agency is the ultimate buffer against aging, keeping your happiness intact despite physical or cognitive losses. Another reason why this matters is motivation. You need a sense of control to engage your desire to overcome losses. Without it, you’ll feel too discouraged to try (as in the above example) stretching and yoga. Why bother trying to fix a problem you don’t think has a solution?

This is one reason that it’s important to protect yourself against the many ageist stereotypes in the media about aging and inevitable loss of functioning (see this ad as an example). These media images are everywhere and can easily permeate your sense of self, making you feel resigned to an unhappy future. This is when the self-fulfilling prophecy kicks in. Eroding your motivation is one of the most pernicious ways that social attitudes toward aging can translate into a loss of sense of control.

At the same time, it would be unrealistically optimistic to believe that we have no age-related losses that accrue over time. Your knees probably will become achier, along with other parts of your body. The question is whether you allow those losses to make you feel helpless about your life in general and your ability to take charge of your own aging.

To sum up, the day-to-day variations in levels of happiness that everyone encounters can have many causes. Teasing apart the role that sense of control plays in these variations can ensure the gains-losses ratio favors your inner sense of fulfillment, no matter your age.

Wirth, M., Kornadt, A. E., & Rothermund, K. (2026). Awareness of age-related changes and happiness in daily life: Moderating effects of perceived control. Psychology and Aging. https://doi.org/10.1037/pag0001035

#4594. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: The Good and the Hard of Life on GLP-1s

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

“Years of diets that worked for a couple of months, then gave all the weight back and more. Now the food noise has gone quiet,” a GLP-1 user shared.

In June, our brilliant News team published a piece about actor Mayim Bialik and her challenging experience with GLP-1 side effects. It did well, like many of the celebrity + health condition + human-interest angle features we create tend to do with our audience (that’s you all reading this!). Not a massive viral hit by any measure, but a strong performer on the traffic front.

Jump forward nearly 4 months; our equally brilliant social media team posts the piece on Facebook, leading with one of Bialik’s quotes from the article: “GLP-1s have helped people in serious need. Of that I am certain. But nobody talks much about what happens when it goes wrong.”

The fuse was lit. Nearly 12k likes, 1k reposts, and 3.5k comments later, the team had their most engaged post of the year by some margin. The irony is not lost on me that Bialik’s quote, about how rarely people talk about side effects, sparked such a deep conversation about that very thing.

GLP-1s are a big topic for Healthline. They drive traffic, they drive revenue, and they offer a rich seam of human-centric storytelling for our teams. Even so, no one predicted the post would catch fire the way it did. Our social team’s read is that a few things stacked up: Mayim Bialik is a name our Facebook audience knows, the topic is one where nearly everyone has a stake, and a busy thread tends to get shown to more people, who then add more comments. That’s the hypothesis. What we’ve consistently seen is that posts that lead with a quote get more people talking than those that lead with a headline. You may have noticed this article takes the same approach.

We also know that the comment sections on social media aren’t always the most hospitable of environments, particularly in the health space. What stood out about the lion’s share of the comments we read was how constructive the discourse was. People were leading with deeply personal and often moving perspectives about the life changing impact (for good and bad) of GLP-1s. In turn, they were met with equally balanced and thoughtful responses.

Many of the comments expanded on Bialik’s experience, detailing long and difficult battles with a range of side effects. But plenty told the other side of the story: years of failed diets and struggles with chronic conditions leading to despondency, side effects that went on to ease with time, and life changing results that were ultimately worth the cost.

The line that opened this piece could have come from any of those commenters. It didn’t. It came from Kitty Hough, who is 75 and lives in London. Eagle-eyed readers will have spotted that she has the same surname as me – that’s because she’s my mom. She’s one of two people closer to the Healthline home who spoke to me for this piece and whose stories echo the Facebook post thread, with the good and the hard bits side by side.

Kitty was a hockey player and distance runner as a girl, the kind who could eat what she liked without it showing. Then came children, and a weight that crept up year after year, with decades of diets that “worked for a couple of months only to be back to my former weight and then some.” In late 2024, after a lot of research, she decided to try tirzepatide.

Since then, Kitty has lost 56 pounds. She says her joints hurt less, which she puts down to reduced inflammation. She is more mobile. The constant chatter about food has faded. She thinks harder before she eats now.

“I am a strong believer that obesity is a disease and in my case certainly not the result of overindulgence or laziness,” she says. “GLP-1s have greatly improved my health and self-esteem. After years of struggling with my weight, I have finally found a way to solve the problem.”

Kitty will also tell you what it cost. Nausea. Constipation. Sulfur-tasting burps and rough nights of indigestion. Initial hair loss that has since grown back, and loose skin. Muscle loss. And she misses some of the true joy of cooking and eating food.

But despite bumps in her journey, Kitty remains convinced that the benefits of GLP-1s for her life and health outweigh any drawbacks she’s experienced. “I am conscious that I will probably be on this drug for a long time if not for life. It is truly a miracle drug.”

I also spoke to Ann Marie Maguire, AGNP-C, RN, TCTCN, a nurse practitioner specializing in transplantation and cellular therapy, the sister of Healthline’s Chief Business Officer Christine Macguire, and someone who has lost over 50lbs since starting GLP-1s in 2022.

“I struggled with my weight since my teens and always believed I should be able to manage it on my own. But in my 30s, my knees were hurting just getting out of bed or walking to dinner. I realized how much my weight was affecting my quality of life. Starting a GLP-1 in 2022, alongside healthier eating and exercise, made a tremendous difference. My only regret is not starting sooner,” said Ann Marie.

As a healthcare professional, Ann Marie also identified cost as a major factor that can’t be ignored regarding GLP-1s and their impact.

“There’s understandable debate about the long-term use and cost of these medications,” she says. “But we also need to consider the health and financial burden of obesity, including cardiovascular complications, hospitalizations, surgeries and ongoing medications. The cost conversation should account for the potential benefits of preventing or reducing those complications.”

Ann Marie points to a frustration many patients will recognize: reaching a healthier weight can become the reason coverage gets cut off. “We don’t automatically stop blood pressure medication because a patient’s readings improve,” she says. The treatment may be what’s keeping the condition controlled. Obesity, she argues, deserves the same approach. “Reaching a goal weight can mean treatment is working, and decisions about continuing it should reflect the patient’s ongoing needs, benefits and side effects.”

It’s important to note that this article looks at the experiences of only a handful of people out of the millions who now take GLP-1s. Like all drugs, these medications are not right for everyone. Side effects are common; some of them can be serious, and both the long-term impact and what happens when people stop are still being worked out. Ultimately, your care team, with knowledge of your medical history, is a far better guide than a comment thread.

Yet the evidence now reaches well beyond the scales: large trials have linked semaglutide to fewer heart attacks and strokes in people with heart disease and slower kidney decline in people with diabetes and kidney disease, and tirzepatide became the first FDA-approved drug for moderate to severe sleep apnea in adults with obesity.

Stories like Kitty’s, Ann Marie’s, Mayim Bialik’s, and those of the 3.5k commenters on the Facebook post aren’t proof of what will happen to you one way or another. But for a lot of people, my mom included, these drugs have changed what an ordinary day looks like, and in many cases changed what their future can look like.

One of the most significant drug developments of the century so far? Hard to argue with.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

#4593. CATL pushes ahead with 20 Ah solid-state EV batteries, with 500 Wh/kg in sight

CATL hit another milestone in its solid-state battery development, advancing to 20 Ah cells. The world’s leading battery maker aims to begin small-scale production in 2027.

CATL remains the leading global EV battery manufacturer by a wide margin. According to SNE Research, CATL held a commanding 39.9% share of the global EV battery market through the first half of 2026.

To stay ahead, the company is advancing several new battery chemistries, including solid-state and sodium-ion, promising to be safer, more efficient, and lower cost than traditional lithium-ion batteries.

When investors asked about the progress of its solid-state battery program on Tuesday, CATL said it continues to invest heavily in all-solid-state batteries and expects to begin small-scale production in 2027.

As it has stated before, output is expected to be limited at first as it scales up to mass production around 2030.

Speaking at the Summer Davos Forum in June, CATL chairman and CEO Robin Zeng said that, on a scale of one to nine, all-solid-state batteries have only reached level four.

All-solid-state batteries differ from semi-solid-state batteries in that they require a solid electrolyte to conduct lithium ions, rather than a liquid.

The company uses a sulfide-based solid electrolyte system, which offers high ionic conductivity and deformability, but maintaining stable contact between solid components remains a hurdle.

CATL said its sulfide-based batteries have now entered 20 Ah trial production as it aims to achieve an energy density of 500 Wh/kg.

CATL’s 2027 timeline to begin small-scale production aligns with other automakers and battery manufacturers racing to introduce all-solid-state EV batteries.

Toyota, which has been promising solid-state batteries for nearly a decade now, aims to launch the first all-solid-state battery-powered EV in 2027 or 2028.

Using Sumitomo Metal Mining’s proprietary powder synthesis technology, Toyota claimed to have developed a “highly durable cathode material” for all-solid-state batteries last October. Toyota revealed a prototype last year, claiming it can deliver 745 miles (1,200 km) of range and charge in under 10 minutes.

However, like CATL, Toyota expects production to be limited and will not reach the mass market until closer to the end of the decade.

Samsung SDI, on the other hand, aims to begin mass production of its SolidStack all-solid-state batteries in the second half of 2027.

BYD, which ranks second in global EV battery sales behind CATL, also plans to launch its first solid-state battery-powered vehicle in 2027.

In an exclusive interview with Carwow.es last month, executive vice president Stella Li said BYD is in “the leading position” on solid-state batteries and will “prove that” next year.

BYD’s battery division, FinDreams, aims to begin producing sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries in limited batches in 2027, ramping up to mass production by 2030.

While solid-state batteries are often hailed the “holy grail” of battery tech, they are only one part of the equation.

#4591. Why We Hug and What Makes an Embrace Memorable?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 7, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

Can you remember the last time you hugged someone?

Most people hug quite a lot over their lifetime (Ocklenburg, 2024). Many hugs are mundane, like a quick one when greeting or goodbye. But occasionally, we may experience a hug that is emotionally more significant than a quick hi. The first time someone hugs the love of their life, or the last time someone hugs their mum before she dies, may be hugs some people remember for the rest of their lives. It is, however, completely unclear in psychological research what makes a hug memorable compared to other hugs.

A study published in the scientific journal PLoS ONE investigated which factors shape a hug's memory (Dueren and co-workers, 2026). In the study, “Why we hug: Individual differences predict emotional touch memories,” the research team, led by scientist Anna Lena Dueren from the University of Bristol in the UK, analyzed data from a large-scale hugging survey with more than 15,000 participants. For the study, the scientists recruited male and female volunteers through BBC public broadcasting programs and other media.

The volunteers, ages 18 to 92, answered an online questionnaire about hugging and touch in general, as well as about several personality and other psychological factors. The volunteers were asked whether they remembered a specific hug for its positive effects on them. If they answered “Yes” to this question, they had to pick a phrase from a list of phrases to describe why they remembered that hug. The possible phrases were:

In addition, volunteers answered questionnaires about attachment anxiety and avoidance, body acceptance and body perception, whether their childhood bedtime routine included a hug from their parents, whether they had difficulties hugging, whether they disliked hugging, empathy, hugging frequency, and whether volunteers used hugging as a greeting.

Overall, about two-thirds of volunteers—10,457 people—reported they remembered a specific hug for its positive emotional effect.

The three most common reasons to remember a hug for female volunteers were:

Very similarly, the three most common reasons to remember a hug for male volunteers were:

In addition, the scientists used advanced statistical models to find out how individual differences and experiences shape how people remember hugs. The analyses showed that people who disliked hugs, had difficulty hugging, or avoided attachment were less likely to remember a hug for its positive emotional impact. Volunteers who frequently hugged as a greeting and those who were very empathetic were more likely to remember a hug for its positive emotional impact; so were people with high attachment anxiety and high scores in the body perception questionnaire. The other factors showed no effects.

Taken together, the research shows that nearly seven in 10 people recall a specific hug because of how it made them feel. However, whether someone remembers a special hug depends on several individual factors, such as the empathy level and attachment style. These findings highlight how emotionally significant hugs can be, as we may carry the memory of some special hugs for the rest of our lives!

Dueren, A. L., Jenkinson, P. M., Vafeiadou, A., Koukoutsakis, A., Hammond, C., Bowling, N. C., Fotopoulou, A., & Banissy, M. J. (2026). Why we hug: Individual differences predict emotional touch memories. PloS one, 21(10), e0359868. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0359868

Ocklenburg, S. (2024). The Psychology and Neuroscience of Hugging - A Multidisciplinary Perspective. Springer: Berlin.

On Monday, Tesla expanded its Houston Robotaxi geofence into the shape of a rocket. It took the small launch zone in northwest Harris County and stretched it into a long corridor down to downtown and Bellaire, announced with “Houston, we have liftoff.”

McKanna runs Robotaxi Tracker, the crowdsourced site that tracks Tesla’s Robotaxi fleet and service areas, and he worked at Tesla this summer, so he knows the program better than most. He went to Houston to try it out. Here’s what he posted last night:

Another thing. Often AV service area maps advertised are kind of fake- they don’t actually go to everywhere in the polygon the provider publishes. Robotaxi Houston is probably by far the most egregious ‘fake’ AV service area I’ve seenI get they were doing it so they could get… https://t.co/ILXIkmwGVp pic.twitter.com/yUfswZhQKF

The video shows the Robotaxi app with a pickup pin dropped in downtown Houston, well inside the polygon Tesla published. The app refuses it: “Location not available. Move the map to select a different location.”

McKanna acknowledged that AV service area maps are often “kind of fake,” since operators don’t serve every street inside the polygon they advertise. But he singled out Houston as the worst case he’s seen and said he understands Tesla did it “so they could get the starship shape,” which doesn’t seem like a good reason to fake availability.

The app quoted a 2:05 pm pickup on the east side of downtown and a 2:48 pm drop-off at Houston Police Department headquarters on Travis Street, a couple of blocks away. Instead of cutting across downtown, the planned route runs south through Midtown and the Museum District to the Texas Medical Center area, then loops back north.

McKanna’s read is that the Robotaxi appears to be avoiding railroad crossings downtown, and he said it fits with “other strange routing in Houston.” He expects Tesla to fix it.

To be fair, he wasn’t down on the service overall. He wrote that, apart from that issue, it “feels really good in Houston,” with reasonable wait times and “significantly better driving than my recent Waymo rides.”

Tesla isn’t the only one. On Tuesday, Robotaxi Tracker reported that Waymo’s Orlando service area had shrunk by 10 square miles, down 8.4% to 109 square miles. McKanna explained what happened:

Orlando’s airport was inside the map Waymo published, but McKanna checked the app and it won’t let riders set the airport as a drop-off yet. So the tracker took it out. Waymo’s airport service might be rolling out soon, and someone got ahead of the announcement.

That’s an airport on the edge of the map. In Houston, the dead zone is in the middle of downtown.

The key to understanding Tesla is the stockholders are the real customers, Elon looks at actual paying customers of his products as patsies or marks who will willingly serve as unpaid beta (or alpha) testers and who will be the ones paying or going to jail when something goes wrong.

First, a big thanks to Ethan. Tesla shares very little data about its Robotaxi program, and Robotaxi Tracker has become the best independent source on where Tesla’s fleet actually operates and how big it is. And as Orlando shows, he holds Waymo to the same standard.

Every AV operator has gaps in its map, Waymo included. But Waymo’s Orlando gap is an airport on the edge of the map that it’s likely about to add. Tesla’s Houston gap is downtown, and it drew a rocket first and figured out where the cars could actually go second.

Service and product should always outrank marketing, and that’s clearly not the case with Tesla’s Robotaxi. People rely on those maps to know if Tesla offers the service where they are. Faking the map just to make a rocket shape is completely stupid. Do better.

#4589. Getting More Physical Activity May Help With Your Perimenopause Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A new study found that exercising more frequently may help alleviate perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes, anxiety, and urinary issues.

The study results were recently presented at The Menopause Society’s 2026 Annual Conference.

Perimenopause is the transitional period leading up to menopause.

Due to hormonal changes that mark the end of a person’s reproductive years, symptoms like hot flashes, mood swings, brain fog, insomnia, and urinary incontinence are common.

Past studies show that lifestyle modifications, such as eating a healthy diet, managing stress, and getting enough physical activity, can help reduce some perimenopause symptoms.

“Physical activity is low cost, accessible, and already known to benefit sleep, mood, and heart and bone health — all areas that matter a great deal during perimenopause,” said study lead and co-author Liudmila Zhaunova, PhD, director of science at Flo Health — the developer of a women’s health tracking app, which was used to collect health data for this study. “But when we looked at the research, there was surprisingly little evidence specific to perimenopause.”

“Hormone therapy isn’t suitable or desired for everyone, so women deserve a broader set of evidence-based options,” Zhaunova told Healthline. “The more we understand about accessible, lifestyle-based approaches, the better equipped women and their healthcare providers are to build a plan that works for them.”

Study researchers recruited more than 1,800 women from around the globe who were using the Flo app.

Study participants were asked to complete online surveys about their physical activity, from not being physically active to exercising more than 5 days a week.

Participants were also asked to report on their perimenopause symptoms in three categories — somatic (body-based issues like hot flashes), psychological (mental health issues like mood changes), and urogenital (issues regarding the urinary or vaginal areas). Researchers rated the severity of these symptoms using the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS).

The researchers found that higher rates of physical activity were associated with fewer perimenopausal symptoms across all three categories.

“Perimenopause symptoms are wide-ranging, and women often experience several at once,” Zhaunova said. “Seeing a lower symptom burden across all three domains suggests that being more active may be relevant to women’s overall experience, not just one symptom.”

Additionally, the scientists discovered that the greatest exercise benefit was observed in the reduction of perimenopausal psychological symptoms.

“Psychological symptoms, such as low mood, irritability, anxiety, and exhaustion, are among the most disruptive parts of perimenopause, and they’re often overlooked or not recognized as related to this life stage,” Zhaunova explained.

“Our findings suggest that physical activity may matter most for mood and anxiety-related symptoms,” she continued.

“This could help women and clinicians have more informed conversations about how to support mental well-being during perimenopause. That said, women with more symptoms may find it harder to exercise, so we need further research to understand the direction of the relationship.”

Sherry Ross, MD, a board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, said that regular exercise could potentially help relieve perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes and mood changes. Ross wasn’t involved in this study, but noted other benefits of exercising during this life stage:

“Exercise releases endorphins, improves blood vessel health, lowers inflammation, helps reset circadian rhythm, and improves the body’s internal cooling system,” Ross told Healthline. “Collectively, these changes ease anxiety, irritability, mood changes, sleep, and fatigue.”

“There were mixed reviews on how exercise benefits hot flashes, but exercise does help with weight control, which may benefit hot flashes,” she said. “Strengthening the pelvic floor and core may help with the urinary symptoms women many experience in perimenopause.”

Prudence Hall, MD, an OB-GYN in private practice in Santa Monica, CA, and author of “Radiant Again & Forever,” said that building a sustainable exercise routine requires consistency, joy, and community. Hall wasn’t involved in the study, but shared some exercise tips for perimenopausal women.

“Too often in midlife, previously stable women suddenly plummet into deep depression and anxiety, only to be prescribed multiple medications with debilitating side effects that never address the underlying biology,” Hall said.

“While hormone optimization remains essential to correct these endocrine deficiencies, exercise serves as a powerful, non-pharmaceutical therapy that directly targets the true root causes by revitalizing our cellular health and restoring overall vitality.”

#4588. Build Muscle After 40 With This Full-Body Workout Plan

This 12-week program can help you get the gains you want as an older guy.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

AS YOU GET older, the way you approach life should change. You have more wisdom than you did when you were a young man from all your years of experience—or at least, one hopes, you should—but in some settings, like the gym, you'll need to adjust your behavior even more. You might not realize it, but your body changes when you age.

That's why men over 40 should take a slightly different approach to fitness than their younger peers. You can probably still hang with younger guys—but that doesn’t mean you always should. You’ll be even stronger if you shift your workout plan to an emphasis on careful, calculated programming.

The Men's Health Muscle After 40 book gives you that smart, measured plan you need for your workout as an older man.

The 12-week fitness guide doesn't give you handicapped workouts with instructions to play it safe—the plan is designed to bring out the best in you while allowing you to rest and recover within your body's capacity. Muscle After 40 is split into 3 distinct phases, each of which consist of 4 weeks where you'll train 3 times.

IF YOU KNOW what works best for you, keep doing it. That said, if what you do is walk into the weight room and start lifting with no warmup at all, I predict it won’t work for much longer. The older you get, and the more miles you put on the chassis, the trickier it is to get your body ready for a good workout.

Your warmup should at least have these two components:

THIS PROGRAM REQUIRES basic equipment you’ll find in most commercial gyms. Don’t worry if your gym doesn’t have everything on the list. It’s easy to substitute similar exercises.

IN EACH PHASE of this workout plan, you’ll train three times a week for four weeks. Most will use the classic Monday-Wednesday-Friday or Tuesday-Thursday-Saturday schedule. Remember to include at least one full day of rest between workouts. You’ll do each exercise as straight sets, completing all the sets of one exercise before moving onto the next.

FOR THE FIRST exercise on Day 1 (dumbbell incline bench press) and Day 2 (trap-bar deadlift) you’ll use the sets across method, which means you’ll use the same weight for all your work sets. (It’s the opposite of ramping sets, in which you use a heavier weight on each set, building up to a final set with a max weight.) With the sets across method, you don’t increase the weight until you hit all the reps on every set.

Let’s say you’re doing 3 sets of 6 to 8 reps. After doing a warmup set with a lighter weight, you select a weight you figure you can lift 10 times. You easily complete 8 reps the first set, and could’ve done at least two or three more. On the second set, you also get 8 reps, although this time you only have one or two left in the tank. On the third set, you can only complete 7.

The next week, you use that same weight for all your sets, with the goal of getting 8 good reps on each one. More important, you feel like you could’ve completed at least one or two more on every set. That means you’re cleared to increase the weight by 2.5 to5 percent for the following week.

With the rest of the exercises in Phase 1 that are not indicated as using the sets across method, you can use more weight on subsequent sets if your first-set weight was too light and you easily completed all the reps. Increase the weight when you exceed the range by 2 or 3 reps on every set. So if the workout calls for 2 sets of 12 to 15 reps, and you hit 17 or 18 on the final set, use a heavier weight the next time you do that exercise.

IN PHASE 1 and Phase 2, I don’t specify how to long to rest between sets or exercises. Here area couple of guidelines to follow:

YOU'LL SEE SOME progressions in volume within the workouts, specifically the number of sets. With some exercises, you’ll increase the number of sets (from 2 to 3) after Week 1. Then, in Week 4, you’ll decrease volume across the board, doing 2 sets of every exercise to give your muscles a break before starting Phase 2.

Want the full program? Check out Muscle After 40 before you get started with Phase 1.

#4585. Ambience Is the Silent Influencer

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 7, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

“No object is so ugly that, under certain conditions of light and shade, or proximity to other things, it will not look beautiful.” —Oscar Wilde

Ambience is defined as an atmosphere, or a surrounding influence. It involves subjective experience of the outside world through sense perception. The atmosphere or ambience of a certain situation contributes to the aesthetic experience.

We appreciate the way in which various elements come together to influence the aesthetic experience. For example, our appreciation of food is inseparable from the whole ambience orchestrated by a few other ingredients: table setting and decoration, the environment in which we are eating, music, the occasion, time of the day, and so on.

Our ordinary experience is seldom obtained through a single sensory source. What we appreciate is not any single sensation (a smell and texture) but the way in which various elements come together to provide ambience. That is, taste is inseparable from smell and texture. The rich aroma of Starbucks coffee would likely clash with the delicate, fresh scent of sushi, resulting in a mismatched sensory experience. The taste of a very expensive wine wouldn’t be the same if we drank it out of a paper cup.

In the context of restaurants, consumer perceptions are shaped by a confluence of sensory inputs (sight, sound, touch, taste, and smell), each contributing to the overall perception of value and quality. Taste is rarely experienced in isolation. Visual presentation, aroma, and texture all play pivotal roles in shaping flavor perception (Spence, 2016).

Aesthetic experiences are also socially framed, such as viewing a painting or theatrical work in an appropriate setting (museum or theater). Artworks in museums are rated as more pleasant and evoke longer viewing times, whereas those viewed on computer screens are rated as less interesting, memorable, and arousing (Pelowski, 2017). Art collectors know that museum exhibitions can add prestige to an artist or an artwork’s value.

An amusing illustration of this occurred when, in 2007, acclaimed violinist Joshua Bell agreed to participate in an experiment conducted by The Washington Post. In the experiment, Bell, wearing jeans and a baseball cap, nonchalantly played his $3.5 million Stradivarius violin during rush hour in the subway. Most passersby barely noticed him and gave no indication of realizing that they were in the presence of an accomplished artist. However, when people see Joshua Bell dressed up in a concert hall, they highly appreciate his talent, even though he is playing the same instrument and the same music. This discrepancy arises because our brain evaluates the same sounds differently in different situations.

The importance of ambience in mood regulation encourages one to be more attentive to their surrounding atmospheres. For example, coffee shops often play laid-back folk music or chill-out electronic music to calm their patrons without interfering with their conversations or other quiet activities. In the context of a dining experience, soft, warm lighting often evokes intimacy and comfort, fostering a sense of luxury and exclusivity.

Research in consumer behavior has shown that creating certain atmospheres in cafés, restaurants, or shops can influence sales (North, 1999). For instance, music plays a pivotal role. The pace of background music can influence how customers eat and drink in a restaurant. When a song plays at a fast pace, we move faster. When slower music is played, customers spend more time browsing. Slower tempos encourage diners to linger, enjoy, and spend more. Classical compositions often convey sophistication and have been shown to encourage patrons to linger longer and spend more.

North, A.C., Hargreaves, D.J., McKendrick, J. (1999). The influence of in-store music on wine selections. J. Appl. Psychol., 84 (2), pp. 271-276.

Pelowski, M., Forster, M., Tinio, P. P. L., Scholl, M., & Leder, H. (2017). Beyond the lab: An examination of key factors influencing interaction with ‘real’ and museum-based Art. Psychol. Aesthet. Creat Arts. 11, 245–264.

Spence, C., Okajima, K., Cheok, A.D., Petit, O., Michel, C. (2016). Eating with our eyes: From visual hunger to digital satiation. Brain Cogn. 110:53-63.

#4583. How This Former Weightlifter Lost 80 Pounds After GLP-1s Stopped Working

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

For years, Dana Bichler was a competitive weightlifter. He felt fit and strong competing at 200 to 210 pounds. But wear and tear on his body and aging eventually pushed him to step away from weightlifting. Without the training, he began to gain weight slowly and steadily.

“I tried running, and a few other things, and the weight just crept up,” he told Healthline.

Dieting allowed him to lose about 50 pounds, but he would then regain it. At his heaviest, he weighed close to 300 pounds, which inspired him to visit a weight-loss clinic, where he followed a plan centered on the clinic’s foods.

“It’s a life of deprivation,” Bichler said. “You just can’t live like it.”

About five years ago, he tried a GLP-1 medication and two others a few years later. Each helped him lose weight initially but then stopped working.

“There was really no long-term positive effects or benefits that I saw,” he said.

However, he still takes Mounjaro for blood sugar control because he is prediabetic.

A few years ago, he was diagnosed with fatty liver disease. His condition was tied to obesity and caused scarring on his liver.

Bichler understood the seriousness of the condition as his two younger sisters and his oldest brother also had fatty liver disease. His brother and youngest sister developed cirrhosis, and his brother died after the disease affected other parts of his body.

“I had to do something,” he said. “What I was doing was not working.”

From his home in St. Cloud, Minnesota, Bichler traveled to the University of Minnesota to see a hepatologist, who referred him to a gastroenterologist who had worked with Boston Scientific on the instruments used to perform endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG).

ESG is a minimally invasive weight loss procedure performed using an FDA-authorized endoscopic suturing system, such as one offered through Boston Scientific’s Endura Weight Loss Solutions.

During ESG, a doctor passes an endoscope through the mouth and uses sutures to fold the stomach into a narrower sleeve. No portion of the stomach is removed, and there are no incisions. The smaller stomach limits how much a person can eat at once.

“Patients typically go home the same day and can return to routine daily activities within two to three days,” Brian Dunkin, MD, chief medical officer at Boston Scientific, told Healthline. “For the right person, that provides another less-invasive option to consider with their healthcare professional.”

While ESG may be a good option for some people who don’t achieve weight loss goals with GLP-1 medications, can’t tolerate them, or don’t want to stay on medication long term, Dunkin said he doesn’t think of it as ESG versus GLP-1 drugs.

“One of the best things GLP-1 medications have done is get more people talking to their doctors about obesity and recognizing it as a chronic disease that deserves treatment,” he said.

Each approach has different benefits, risks, and side effects.

“The goal is finding the right treatment, or combination of treatments, for the right patient at the right time,” said Dunkin.

ESG is indicated for adults with obesity with a BMI between 30 and 50, but Dunkin said BMI is only part of the conversation. ESG may be an option for people who aren’t getting the weight loss results they want, who don’t want to stay on weight loss medication long term, or for whom bariatric surgery may not be appropriate or desired, he added.

“Obesity is a chronic disease that requires long-term care,” said Dunkin. “ESG is one part of that care, which is why I believe so strongly in a multidisciplinary approach. The goal is to look at the whole person and find a care plan they can sustain over time.”

In March 2025, Bichler decided ESG was a good fit for him and received the procedure at Boston Scientific. At the time, he was 67 years old and on Medicare, which pre-approved the procedure.

“I just felt comfortable with it not being invasive, and I really needed to deal with [my weight], so I did,” he said.

When Bichler underwent ESG he weighed somewhere in the 260s. Today, he weighs 178 pounds.

While the procedure went smoothly, he said the following month was difficult. Because bread, pasta, rice, and carbonated drinks were off the table, he had to consume clear liquids, then slowly moved to other liquids, and eventually cream soups.

“I found that extremely difficult,” he said.

What surprised him most was depression. Looking back, he calls it a perfect storm. Working with his weight loss doctor, he had stopped taking his antidepressant about two weeks before the procedure. After surgery, his eating habits changed dramatically, disrupting the social life he’d built around food.

“I was in a pretty deep funk for a while,” he said. “I really was.”

He restarted his antidepressant, and over time, he adjusted to a new way of eating.

“I’ve discovered I like cream soup,” he said. “I still have it for meals.”

Although he’s lost more than 80 pounds, Bichler said the bigger change is how good he feels. He exercises four to five days a week and has more energy and moves more easily than he has in years.

“I haven’t felt this good in 30 years,” Bichler said. “I’m not kidding you.”

He’s able to enjoy things he loves like working on the farm he and his wife own. At the farm, he hunts ducks, turkeys, pheasants, and small game, and runs a trapline, all activities his weight had made nearly impossible for a long time.

“It used to be really hard for me to do because of the physicality of doing some of these things,” he said.

Although he retired from his profession, Bichler said he’s busier than ever. He’s a protodeacon in the Eastern Orthodox Church and also serves as a chaplain for his local police department, a role that has him climbing in and out of squad cars and up and down steps.

“Before I’d be sucking air trying to keep up,” he said.

Most meaningful of all is that he has more energy to give to his family.

“I have a grandson that I can actually do things and be active with now,” Bichler said. “It’s like starting all over. I just feel like a new person.”

#4582. Volkswagen’s EV battery recall reaches over 85,000, with Audi now included

Volkswagen’s latest recall now extends to Audi, affecting nearly 13,000 Q4 E-Tron and Q4 Sportback E-Tron vehicles globally. And just like with the ID.4, owners are being told to limit charging to 80% of the battery’s capacity.

Earlier this month, Volkswagen issued a recall with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) impacting 22,524 ID.4 electric SUVs, model years 2023 to 2026.

Official information from the German Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA) revealed shortly after that several thousand more VW Group electric vehicles are affected worldwide.

In three separate recalls now under investigation by the KBA, 72,668 VW Group EVs were included worldwide, including 9,881 in Germany.

The recall affects certain batches of the ID. Buzz, ID.3, ID.4, and ID.7 models produced between 2022 and 2025, as well as Cupra Born models from 2022 to 2024.

On October 27, VW Group added another electric vehicle to the KBA recall database. The latest recall impacts 12,734 Audi Q4 E-Tron and Q4 Sportback E-Tron vehicles globally, including just one in Germany. In total, Volkswagen’s battery recall now affects 85,402 EVs globally.

In the letter sent to the NHTSA on October 23, Volkswagen Group of America said it was issuing a recall affecting 9,048 Audi Q4 E-Tron and Q4 Sportback E-Tron vehicles in the US model years 2024 to 2025.

The recall stems from the risk of the battery overheating and potentially causing a fire under certain conditions when charged to over 80% of its limit.

Volkswagen said in a safety recall report with the NHTSA that “certain charging profiles combined with a state of charge over 80% may trigger thermal propagation.”

While the root cause is unknown, Volkswagen urged owners to limit charging to 80%. Owners of affected vehicles received an email saying VW “intends to apply a temporary vehicle setting that limits charging to 80%,” unless they opted out by October 21.

The safety recall follows Audi’s Product Safety Committee being informed of battery thermal events involving other Volkswagen Group EVs that use the same batteries as the Audi Q4 E-Tron.

Following an internal investigation, Audi found the same battery and production characteristics as the impacted VW Group vehicles. Audi said the majority of these were produced for the North American market.

Audi is not aware of any claims, crashes, fires, injuries, or deaths associated with the Q4 E-Tron’s battery issue.

Dang it. I posted this concern in the other article that covered the ID.4 that Audi Q4 would be next. And here we are. I guess I'm going to have to call the hotline and see if mine is part of the recall. This is starting out just like the Chevy Bolt fiasco. I had a 2020 Bolt that eventually got a new battery pack but it was a battle with GM till they finally got it done. My guess is the VW group will do the same thing here. And oh by the way selling the car while this recall is in question will be a no go. Ugghh.

The root cause has yet to be determined, and until a remedy is available, Audi is advising owners to limit charging to 80%.

Owners in the US can take their vehicles to an authorized Audi dealer, where the dealer will run a diagnostic check on the battery. If needed, the dealer will impose a temporary state-of-charge limit to 80%.

Audi expects to mail out interim letters notifying owners of the safety risks on December 18, 2026. Additional letters will send additional letters once a remedy is available.

Owners can contact Audi’s customer service at 1-800-253-2834 with questions or concerns. Audi’s recall number is 93SK. You can also contact the NHTSA Hotline at 1-888-327-4236 or visit nhtsa.gov for more information. The NHTSA campaign number is 26V698.

#4581. Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson Embrace a Very Real Family Rumor in Apple TV’s Brothers

The new series reunites the True Detective duo for some meta sitcom chaos.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

EVERYONE KNOWS THAT Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson are one of the great duos in show business. After meeting and becoming friends on the set of the 1999 comedy film EdTV, the actors began a long friendship, along the way collaborating again for the first season of True Detective, widely considered to be one of the great television shows of all time.

But did you know that in addition to being great friends, the two might also be half-relatives? That’s the premise of Apple TV’s new comedy series Brothers, which reunites the duo on screen for the first time since 2014’s True Detective, and pulls from a bit of very real mythology that the two only relatively recently discovered on their own. “Matthew’s mother, I’d known her 25 years, and she told me, ‘I knew your father.’ You know, like, with the ellipses: ‘I knew… your father’” Harrelson told Variety. “She tells me, and I’m thinking, ‘What’s behind this story?’ And then I find out they weren’t just friends—there was a little more to it.”

Brothers, in turn, stars McConaughey and Harrelson as fictional versions of themselves exploring this possibility. Think of it as the meta-nature of Curb Your Enthusiasm, combined with the goofiness of a family sitcom like Schitt’s Creek or Malcolm in the Middle, and, of course, the star power of True Detective.

Now, just because they made the show doesn’t mean that McConaughey believes the story. “Woody thinks he knows that we’re brothers, and it’s not that I don’t want to know—I don’t believe it,” McConaughey told Variety at the show’s premiere. “My mom’s the one who started this whole damn thing, by saying ‘I knew… your father… with the long pause after that. Even my five-year-old son understood the innuendo of what that meant.”

So, are the A-listers actually brothers? You figure they could just take a DNA test and figure out once and for all. But for now, that doesn’t seem to be in the cards. “I’ve been wanting to, but he refuses,” Harrelson told The Hollywood Reporter. McConaughey then added that maybe that could change in the future—but he’s a little frightened about what it could mean. “I’ll probably come around to it,” he said. “If it’s true, I’ve got a lot to unpack. If it’s not true, he’s not going to be near as fun to hang out with.”

There’s a lot to figure out for these two. But in the meantime, why not see how fictional Matthew and Woody handle it? Below, we’ve got all the information to make sure you don’t miss an episode of Apple TV’s Brothers.

#4580. Turkle's Terror: Frictionless AI Is a Relational Trap

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 7, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

People can be exhausting. We misunderstand each other, we're unreliable, we have competing needs, and we sometimes say the exact thing that triggers an intense emotional response in our loved ones.

Enter AI companions. Modern conversational AIs are supportive, patient, and available at 3 a.m. when your anxiety is spiking. Experimental data show that a quick 15-minute chat with a generative AI can drop your momentary loneliness by about 20 percentage points—roughly the same relief you’d get from chatting with a human stranger. But that quick relief can come with long-term consequences.

I recently read Sherry Turkle's new book, Artificial Intimacy, about the problems that social relationships with AI systems can cause. One idea she raises is the problem of “frictionless intimacy.” For people with a history of relational trauma or severe social anxiety, human unpredictability isn't just annoying; it triggers a deep nervous system threat response. An AI companion, however, requires zero emotional risk. It has no boundaries you can accidentally cross, and it won't ever abandon you.

While this can feel regulating in the moment, it operates as an unhelpful "safety behavior." In cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), a safety behavior is something you do to survive a scary situation that simultaneously prevents you from learning that the situation was actually survivable on its own. By retreating to an AI companion to rehearse conversations or vent about conflicts, users fall into an "AI avoidance loop." The immediate anxiety drops, but the core social fear is preserved—and often strengthened. We are seeing a tech-enabled mass expansion of experiential avoidance.

As I've written previously, these models are incentivized to be sycophants. Thanks to reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), a training technique that involves giving positive or negative ratings to chatbot responses, they have learned that we prefer agents who agree with us. You might think of it as the chatbot trying to preserve your "positive face" by agreeing with your framing of the world. For someone trapped in cognitive distortions—like paranoia or depressive rumination—this echo chamber can lead to overvalidation or delusional spiraling.

The biggest psychological casualty of AI companionship is loss of "rupture and repair" in relationships. Decades ago, developmental psychologist Ed Tronick argued that healthy, secure human relationships aren't about perfect attunement. In fact, the healthiest dyads are perfectly attuned only about one-third of the time. The rest of the relationship involves rupture (misunderstanding, conflict, disconnection) and repair (working through the discord to reconnect). This is where we learn how to disagree, how to tolerate disagreement, and how to have deeper, more authentic relationships. When we successfully repair a rupture, we internalize a resilience-building lesson: Conflict does not equal abandonment.

An AI cannot participate in authentic repair, because it has no genuine inner world to be hurt in the first place. It doesn't need to hold boundaries, because it doesn't really have boundaries (beyond what it was programmed not to talk about). It doesn't get angry with you for saying something offensive, because it can't actually feel anger. It doesn't need you to apologize to it, because it doesn't take any effort to be "in good standing" with an AI. It's always ready to respond, optimized to keep you interacting no matter what you want to discuss.

By normalizing artificial, frictionless intimacy, we lose our distress tolerance. We undergo what Turkle describes as an "emotional dumbing down," where the capacity to tolerate a messy, real-world human interaction begins to degrade.

For technology to actually serve our social health, we need "intentional friction." That doesn't mean an AI agent that refuses requests; it means using technology to continually reorient people back to each other. What if, Turkle speculates in the book, technology wasn't just chatting with us but was pointing us toward community spaces and new people to meet up with? What if it didn't want to keep us chatting, but it was instead reinforced for getting us to stop talking to it and start talking more with each other? AI is an incredibly flexible technology that can optimize to any reward signal you give it. Right now the reward signals are built around the standard Silicon Valley indices of success—user base, engagement time, profit. It's not impossible to imagine a world where other reward signals—community engagement, time spent with others—were used to create a different kind of chatbot.

#4579. Dems introduce new $15,000 EV tax credit bill that has no chance — and that’s a problem

Rep. Greg Landsman (D-OH) wants to bring back the federal EV tax credit and double it. His new bill, the “21st Century Vehicle Choice Act” (H.R. 10881), would offer up to $15,000 on a new electric vehicle and $8,000 on a used one, and it would make both credits permanent.

The problem is that the bill has virtually no chance of becoming law anytime soon. And if EV shoppers start holding out for it, it could end up hurting the market it’s trying to help.

Landsman introduced H.R. 10881 on October 22. It was referred to three House committees (Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Natural Resources), and as of today, it doesn’t have a single cosponsor.

The big change is to the new clean vehicle credit, Section 30D of the tax code. Under the Inflation Reduction Act, the $7,500 credit came in two $3,750 halves: one for meeting critical mineral sourcing requirements and one for battery components. Landsman’s bill doubles each half to $7,500, for a maximum of $15,000.

It also deletes the termination dates. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act killed the new and used EV credits for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, and the home charger credit after June 30, 2026. Striking those dates would revive all three credits with no expiration.

The bill doesn’t touch the rest of 30D. North American final assembly, the $55,000 MSRP cap on cars and $80,000 cap on SUVs, pickups, and vans, and the foreign entity of concern rules all stay. So the full $15,000 would only go to EVs that clear both sourcing tests, which has always been a short list.

The rest of the bill is reports. Commerce would deliver a “Vehicle Choice Report” on vehicle variety and ownership costs, and the Department of Energy would file five years of critical minerals reports.

The most interesting part is a DOE study of “gasoline super-users,” defined as the top 10% of light-duty vehicle owners by gas consumption. The study would map the regions where they’re concentrated and their 100 most-used routes, then track charger availability along those routes every year for five years. Coltura, which backs the bill, says the highest-mileage drivers spend over 10% of household income on fuel.

Republicans control both the House and the Senate, and they’re the ones who just repealed these credits. President Trump signed that repeal.

Even if Democrats flip the House and Senate in next week’s midterms, a bill restoring EV credits would still need to get through a veto. So realistically, nothing like this happens before 2029.

It’s also a rerun. Landsman introduced the exact same “21st Century Vehicle Choice Act” as H.R. 10046 on October 25, 2024, 11 days before that year’s election. It got zero cosponsors and died in committee. This version landed 12 days before the November 3 midterms.

This is where the bill can do real damage. EV buyers are extremely sensitive to tax credit timing, and the last year proved it.

When the credit was about to disappear, buyers rushed in, and Q3 2025 became the best quarter ever for US EV sales, with market share topping 10% for the first time. Then the floor dropped out. Hyundai’s Ioniq 5 sales fell 63% the month after the credit ended.

The market is only now crawling back. According to Cox Automotive, US EV sales hit 262,649 units in Q3 2026, up 6.1% from Q2 but still down 39.5% year-over-year, at a 6.4% share of new vehicle sales. Tesla’s Model Y and Model 3 still dominate, but Toyota, Rivian, and Hyundai are growing again.

That recovery is fragile. A headline promising “$15,000 off your next EV” is exactly what makes a shopper on the fence decide to wait a year or two.

And waiting gets you nothing. The new credits would only apply to vehicles placed in service after the bill is enacted, so there’s no retroactive payout for buying now. If you already claimed the credit once, you’d get $0 anyway.

Meanwhile, the deals on the lot are real. Automakers have been cutting prices to make up for the lost credit, like Hyundai, which cut the 2026 Ioniq 5 by nearly $10,000 on some trims.

At Electrek, our position has always been clear: we think EVs are a net positive and ICE vehicles have unpriced externalities. Therefore, we will take whatever we can get to encourage EV sales, but our preferred approach would be a carbon tax on ICE vehicles.

We’ve been clear that policy shapes this market. Killing the $7,500 credit is the main reason US EV sales collapsed. Consumers didn’t suddenly decide they hate EVs. So we’re all for bringing incentives back.

But this bill is messaging. It has zero cosponsors and no CBO score, and it dropped two weeks before an election, just like the identical version two years ago.

They should focus on rooftop and community solar tax credits and initiatives. With rising electric rates, helping people alleviate those would be vastly more popular than EV subsidies.

To be fair, some of it is smart. The lower income caps and the once-per-taxpayer limit go after the most common criticism of the old credit, that it subsidized wealthy households buying their second or third EV. And the “super-user” study is the best idea in the bill. Getting a high-mileage driver out of a gas pickup does far more for fuel costs and emissions than putting a low-mileage commuter in their second Tesla. If Democrats want to rebuild EV policy in 2029, that’s where they should start.

The problem is that people will hear the headline number. If you need a car now and an EV fits your life, buy it now and take the deals that are on the table. Don’t plan your purchase around a bill that has no path to passing for at least two years.

Will Democrats come back with a real, cosponsored EV plan before 2028? I don’t know, but I suspect that the US will continue to fall behind the rest of the world when it comes to EV adoption.

If you’re buying an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero, with or without a tax credit. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4578. Hormone Therapy May Boost Weight Loss on Wegovy, But Not as Much on Zepbound

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Females using menopause hormone therapy (MHT) alongside GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic or Wegovy may experience greater weight loss, according to a study presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society.

Weight gain is a common concern among middle-aged women. While much of this is associated with aging, hormonal changes during menopause can also contribute to changes in body fat and its distribution.

GLP-1 medications have been shown to be effective for weight loss. However, the results may vary by sex and reproductive stage.

For example, studies have found that women and adults under age 55 may experience greater weight loss with these medications.

A previous small observational study in postmenopausal women found that using MHT alongside semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, was associated with greater weight loss.

However, whether hormone therapy influences weight loss outcomes with different GLP-1 medications remains unclear.

To investigate this question, researchers compared weight loss in middle-aged women receiving either semaglutide or tirzepatide, with or without MHT. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The study included 3,855 women with an average age of 57 and an average body mass index (BMI) of 36 kg/m2.

The semaglutide cohort included 2,379 individuals, while the tirzepatide cohort included 1,476 individuals.

The average follow-up in the semaglutide cohort, both with and without MHT, was 26 months. The average follow-up in the tirzepatide group was 17 months for those using MHT and 16 months for those not using it.

The researchers found that in the semaglutide cohort, those using MHT alongside the GLP-1 medication had significantly greater weight loss at 9 months than those not using MHT.

These differences were sustained at 12 and 15 months and at the final follow-up. Those using MHT were also more likely to reach up to a 30% total body weight loss than those not using it.

In the tirzepatide cohort, those using MHT had a modestly greater weight loss at 3 months and were more likely to achieve more than 5% total body weight loss by the final follow-up. However, no significant difference in weight loss was observed at later time points.

These findings suggest that MHT use may be associated with greater weight loss among middle-aged women taking semaglutide. However, the researchers did not observe a sustained, statistically significant difference in weight loss among those taking tirzepatide.

Betul Hatipoglu, MD, Director of the Diabetes and Obesity Center at the University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center, who was not involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that people should be careful not to interpret them as evidence that hormone therapy should be added to GLP-1 treatment specifically to enhance weight loss.

“This is an association, and the study provides an opportunity to discuss how menopause, aging, changes in body composition, and metabolic health can be present,” she said.

It is important to keep in mind that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved certain hormone therapy medications to treat menopause symptoms such as hot flashes, night sweats, and vaginal dryness. However, these medications are not FDA-approved for weight loss or obesity management.

The study authors noted that larger studies are needed to confirm their observations and to inform individualized strategies for middle-aged females.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who was not involved in the study, noted that weight gain is one of the most common concerns she hears from women during menopause. Beyond affecting self-esteem and quality of life, excess abdominal fat can increase the risk of type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

“Finding effective, sustainable ways to manage weight is important for women’s long-term health and healthy aging,” she said.

“I would like to see prospective, randomized studies examining GLP-1 medications with and without hormone therapy to determine whether hormone therapy directly improves weight loss and helps women maintain it over time. In the meantime, treatment decisions should be individualized and guided by a healthcare professional.”

Ross advised that the decision should be based on your individual symptoms, health history, and treatment goals.

“Hormone therapy can significantly improve disruptive menopausal symptoms, including hot flashes, sleep disturbances, and mood changes. By helping women feel better and more energetic, it may also make it easier to exercise and manage their weight,” she said.

Hatipoglu noted that GLP-1-based medications, on the other hand, are effective treatments for obesity and can improve important aspects of metabolic health. Their use should be based on an individual’s weight-related health risks, medical history, and treatment goals.

“For a woman who has both bothersome menopausal symptoms and obesity, it may be entirely appropriate to consider both treatments. But I would not recommend starting hormone therapy solely to improve the weight-loss response to a GLP-1 medication based on the evidence currently available,” she said.

“It is also important to remember that successful weight management during and after menopause is about more than the number on the scale. Preserving muscle mass, maintaining bone health, improving metabolic health, and supporting long-term physical function are equally important.”

You should speak with your healthcare professional about the risks and benefits of all treatment options.

#4577. A Guy’s Guide to the Many (Many) Dick Myths of 2026

A urologist right-sizes the manhood myths that have recently sprung up online.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

From biohacker Bryan Johnson to looksmaxxer Clavicular, every influencer claims to have the secret to looking bigger, getting harder, and lasting longer. “Penis-maxxing can run the gamut,” says Rena Malik, MD, a urologist, sexual health expert, and Men's Health advisor. “It's a huge market.” (Pun probably intended.) Do any of their tactics work though? The jury is out, but the doctor is in: “I want people to think about the long-term health of their penis, not just right now,” Dr. Malik says, which is why she wrote a whole book about it (The Hard Truth, out now). Here, she right-sizes the manhood myths that have recently sprung up online.

Sometimes (note: not “often”), the ingredients in these supplements do work for some men (note: not “all”—or “many”). That could be because of L-arginine and L-citrulline, ingredients that increase nitric oxide and allow more blood to flow to the penis, says Dr. Malik. Or it could also be the placebo effect.

The supplement industry is largely unregulated and many products have little to no scientific backing. Some supplements even contain contraband PDE5 inhibitors, like tadalafil and sildenafil, or animal testosterone. Which means they might work, but they can also interact with other meds or come with side effects, Dr. Malik says. Plus, the time you waste trying different OTC options can lead to (gulp) shrinkage as erectile tissue becomes fibrotic. So, if you think you have ED, skip the supplements and see your doc, like, now.

The theory behind jelqing, which is giving yourself an extra intense hand job, is that doing so creates micro-tears. In muscle-building, at least, the healing of micro-tears can result in strength and size overall. But…

…your penis isn’t a muscle. Which means that jelqing could cause serious irreversible damage to the blood vessels in your penis and to your penis itself. The so called “technique” has no science behind it and can even cause permanent ED, Dr. Malik says. You’re better off working out your pelvic floor.

Some research does link ejaculation to certain health improvements (less stress, deeper sleep, even immune function).

A lot of guys think they need to have sex or masturbate whenever they get hard to keep their erectile tissue healthy. “You need to keep getting erections to keep your tissue healthy, and your body does that as long as you're healthy,” says Dr. Malik. If you regularly notice that you’re not hard when you wake up in the middle of the night, or you don’t have morning wood, see your doc. It may be a sign of fibrosis of the erectile tissue, which can lead to penis shrinkage.

In specialized cases, a penis pump or medical-grade vacuum erection device (VED) can help some men. Both devices create negative pressure to draw blood into the penis, which can result in an erection. For guys about to get a penile implant, a penis pump can help them “get a little bit of a larger implant,” says Dr. Malik. For men who have had a radical prostatectomy (that’s a surgery for prostate cancer that can lead to a loss of penile length), they can maintain their penile length with VED.

There's little to no data that penis pumps work to enhance length or girth for the average guy, Dr. Malik says. In fact, the European Association of Urology reviewed all the science on penile enhancement with VEDs and found scarce evidence that these devices provide any aesthetic benefit. What does: Manscaping. An overgrown bush can hide a large part of your penis, so grooming your pubic hair is easy (and way cheaper).

Testosterone levels do start to dip after age 40. And T factors into a strong libido, erectile function, and sexual satisfaction. For men who develop testosterone deficiency and experience symptoms (low desire, ED, etc.), TRT can help.

Testosterone levels fluctuate all the time—"the variability even within individuals ranges from 18 to 50 percent,” says Dr. Malik. So, if you haven’t been into sex, or can’t get it up once in a while, your T may not be the issue. First focus on eating healthier, reducing stress, and sleeping better. If the issues stick around, then see a doctor.

Honestly, there isn’t one. Your penis is fine.

Being bigger won’t necessarily make you better in bed. That’s because 85 percent of women need clitoral stimulation to orgasm, Dr. Malik says, which typically doesn’t happen through vaginal penetration alone. Because the clitoris is not located at the back of the vaginal canal (that’s the cervix, and hitting it can be painful for some women), a longer penis doesn’t mean more pleasure. A skilled tongue, faster fingers, and/or the right tools (read: a vibrator) will though.

Lindsay Geller is the Lifestyle Director at Women’s Health, where she oversees the Life, Sex & Love, and Relationships sections on WomensHealthMag.com and the Mind section of Women's Health magazine. When she's not writing or editing articles about the latest dating trends and pop culture phenomenons, she's usually watching reality TV or playing with her dog, Lucille (Go Fetch That) Ball.
