#4576. Used EVs are suddenly hot sellers — Here are the top SUVs for under $25,000

Don’t want to pay full price? Used EVs with low miles, like the Hyundai IONIQ 5 and Ford Mustang Mach-E, are selling on the secondhand market for $25,000 or less.

With a flood of electric cars returning from lease this year and soaring gas prices, used EVs are suddenly flying off the lot.

Used EV sales rose to a record 3.3% of total used vehicle sales last month, up from 2.9% in August, according to Cox Automotive.

Used ICE vehicle sales, on the other hand, dropped 4.4% in September as buyers flocked to more efficient options.

As expected, Tesla remains the leading used EV brand, followed by Ford, Chevrolet, Hyundai, and BMW.

By model, the Nissan Ariya led growth, with sales up 42.5% in September, followed by the Chevy Equinox EV (+41.9%), Kia EV9 (+36.2%), and Chevy Blazer EV (+30.2%), while the Ford Mustang Mach-E (+14.7%) and Tesla Model Y (+13.8 %) also saw more demand.

With more options to choose from, which one is best for you? To help you decide, Edmunds, which has tested nearly all of them, put together a list of four top used electric SUVs available for under $25,000.

The first one on the list was the Chevy Equinox EV, or as GM used to call it, “America’s most affordable 315+ range” electric vehicle.

After it arrived in 2024, the Chevy Equinox EV quickly became one of the top-selling electric vehicles in the US outside Tesla, winning over buyers with enough space for a family and plenty of driving range at an affordable price.

The Chevy Equinox EV offers up to 319 miles of EPA-estimated driving range. It’s a great fit for those looking for a smaller, more efficient SUV that still offers plenty of interior space.

Edmunds says it’s worth upgrading to the 2LT trim, which adds heated front seats and a heated steering wheel, a wireless phone charger, adaptive cruise control, and a 360-degree HD Surround Vision camera system.

Next on the list was the Ford Mustang Mach-E, which has also remained a top seller since it went on sale in 2021.

Ford tapped into its iconic Mustang nameplate to help attract new buyers. The Mustang Mach-E came well equipped with a large 15.5″ infotainment screen with Wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto and Ford Co-Pilot360 Assist+.

While the GT is the most fun to drive, Edmunds said the Premium trim may be your best bet. It still offers plenty of performance while adding standard features like heated front seats and a heated steering wheel.

It’s also worth upgrading to the extended-range battery pack, which offers up to 320 miles of range on the Premium RWD model. You should be able to find used 2021 to 2023 Mach-E’s for under $25,000.

Another top-selling electric SUV, the Hyundai IONIQ 5 continues to win over buyers with its bold design, long-range capabilities, fast charging, and a surprisingly spacious interior.

Edmunds says plenty of used 2022 to 2024 IONIQ 5s with low mileage are available for under $25,000.

While the base SE Standard Range is the cheapest, it only offers an EPA range of 220 miles. Upgrading to the Extended Range battery, which is used on all other trims, provides up to 303 miles of range.

The Volkswagen ID.4 went on sale in the US in 2021 as one of the earlier mainstream electric SUVs.

It also just happens that many EVs are coming off lease so the inventory is plentiful combined with high gas price. Perfect storm.

It was updated in 2024, but up until the 2023 model year, the VW ID.4 offered an EPA range of up to 275 miles, depending on the configuration.

Finding a low-mileage used 2023 ID.4 shouldn’t be hard, but upgrading to the Pro S trim might be worth it.

Volkswagen updated the 2023 ID.4 with a new 12″ infotainment display and Park Assist Plus. The Pro S trim gained a fixed panoramic roof, V-Tex synthetic leather seating, and a heated steering wheel.

#4575. What Are You Afraid Would Happen If You Changed?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 7, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

Have you ever wished it was easier to say “no” to requests you really didn’t want to do? What about wishing you were better at delegating or asking for help? Or maybe you’ve wondered what life would be like if you were a little bit more fun-loving and carefree.

You know shifting these traits would be good for you, but when the opportunity arises to choose a different response (someone asks you to take the lead on a new project), you stay stuck in the same old patterns (saying “yes” when you’re already overloaded).

We tend to think about change in terms of what we stand to gain. But sometimes, what keeps us stuck is what we're afraid we might lose.

Your personality is your characteristic way of thinking, feeling, and behaving. Often, the personality traits that cause problems for us also come with some clear advantages.

For example, people who are extremely high in conscientiousness might recognize that they’re exhausted from trying to do everything perfectly. At the same time, their attention to detail has also earned them praise, good grades, and later, professional recognition. Choosing good enough over perfect sounds like a great way to decrease burnout, but what would actually happen if they relaxed their standards or delegated a task to someone else?

Or consider someone who is high in neuroticism, the personality trait associated with frequent negative emotions. They might wish they could let their guard down more, but they may also believe that worrying helps them anticipate problems and avoid mistakes. But what would happen if they let themselves enjoy the present? Is that when the other shoe would drop?

These examples demonstrate how even when we recognize that a personality trait is creating difficulties, we may be reluctant to give up the benefits we associate with it.

One reason personality change can feel threatening is that we don't know exactly what will happen when we start behaving differently.

If you've spent years avoiding conflict, you have very little data on how expressing your needs can actually improve relationships. If you've always prepared extensively or worked on tasks until they were perfect, you haven’t had the opportunity to learn that giving 80 percent of your all still earns you praise, or that making a mistake is survivable.

Without collecting these data, your hypotheses about what could happen continue to sound convincing.

If I stop worrying, something important will slip through the cracks.

If I put myself out there, I'll embarrass myself.

These negative predictions make it more likely that you’ll stay in your lane by saying “yes,” overachieving, or keeping quiet about your needs. Staying in your comfort zone provides immediate relief from the possibility of something going wrong. But it also means you continue to lose opportunities to discover whether your predictions are accurate.

Over time, we can become increasingly convinced that our familiar way of doing things is the only safe option, even when it's keeping us from living the way we'd like.

Fortunately, taking baby steps outside your comfort zone can start the cascade of personality change.

Start by identifying a specific behavior you'd like to change and what you’re afraid will happen if you do. Then design a small experiment to test that prediction.

For example, if you're worried that people will be upset when you express a preference, try suggesting the restaurant the next time you make dinner plans with a friend. If you're concerned that relaxing your standards will lead to disaster, try spending a little less time polishing an email before sending it.

Pay attention to what actually happens. Did the consequence you feared occur?

One experiment probably won't change a deeply ingrained personality pattern. But as you collect more data (i.e., repeatedly try out new behaviors and see what happens), you have more to work with when it comes to updating your expectations. And, over time, you'll start to become more comfortable shifting your default responses.

Of course, sometimes the things we're afraid of actually happen.

If you experiment with being more assertive, someone might be disappointed when you say no. If you become less perfectionistic, you might make a mistake. If you put yourself out there socially, you might experience rejection.

It's your job to decide whether the potential benefits of behaving differently are worth taking those risks.

For example, someone working on becoming less agreeable might decide that being able to express their needs in a relationship is worth occasionally disappointing their partner. Someone trying to become less perfectionistic might decide that having more time for their family is worth submitting work that's good enough rather than flawless.

These decisions become easier when we're clear about why we want to change in the first place. Instead of asking whether a new behavior is completely devoid of risks, we can ask whether it moves us closer to the kind of life we want.

Changing can be scary, especially when your familiar behaviors have helped you in the past. But becoming more assertive doesn't mean you have to stop being kind, just as becoming less perfectionistic doesn't mean you have to stop caring about doing good work. Personality change is about having more flexibility in how you respond so that fear of what might happen doesn't keep you from becoming the person you want to be.

You don't have to overhaul your personality to find out what might happen if you behaved differently. My Personality Action Plan helps you identify a small, strategic behavior change that can move you closer to the person you want to become.

#4574. Dutch startup Elysian says electric flight may be closer than you think

They day you get to book an all-electric flight may be closer than you think if Dutch startup Elysian Aircraft gets its way. Their new E9X commercial airliner promises flights that are a whole lot quieter, and at prices that are whole lot less dependent on dumb oil wars.

Aircraft account for more than 2% of global heating when CO₂ and other emissions are taken into account, with the share considerably higher in wealthy countries, according to data cited by climate campaign group Stay Grounded. Elysian Aircraft is keenly aware of the industry’s climate impact, and they believe their planned full-size electric airliner will be perfectly positioned to make a dramatic difference.

“By being able to transport 90 passengers for initially 800 kilometers and eventually 1,000 kilometers you can reduce emissions to zero, from half the world’s flights,” Elysian co-founder Daniel Jacobson told EuroNews. “That is a very large amount of flight activity in the world. And you reduce total emissions from aerospace by 20%.”

At the core of those ambitious emission-reduction goals is the Elysian E9X aircraft. Designed in collaboration with aerospace researchers at Delft University of Technology (TU Delft), the E9X packs its oversized wings with modular battery packs, sending power to six propellers driven by electric motors.

Specs on those haven’t been revealed, but the E9X is designed to carry up to 100 passengers up to 1,000 km (~620 miles) from where they started. Elysian says that’s enough range to handle nearly 50% of scheduled commercial passenger flights worldwide and potentially eliminate 20% of total in-flight emissions when the plane enters service in 2034.

That said, the E9X is far more than “just a concept,” and Elysian has completed its second conceptual design review and flown a scaled demonstrator in concert with Germany’s DLR aerospace research center, demonstrating how its unique battery packaging solutions address the challenges of integrating heavy battery packs into an aircraft’s wings (where fuel is traditionally stored).

It’s interesting to see all the comments that point out the difficulties and problems associated with the introduction of battery powered aircraft into the mainstream industry. What none of them address is the industry’s obsession with cutting their operating costs no matter what pain passengers and flight crews must endure. My bet is if the airlines can save money by converting to battery powered aircraft—there are NO obstacles that will stop them from doing it. Battery electric aircraft may reduce operating costs by thousands of dollars per flight. That alone tells me that they will be flying passengers as soon as possible.

The company is also working with airline partners KLM and Transavia to explore the operational and commercial requirements for putting electric airliners into service, with aircraft lessor TrueNoord investigating how the E9X could be financed and supported commercially.

#4573. I Play Rocky Tells Sylvester Stallone’s Underdog Story. Here’s What Really Happened.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

The new biopic revisits the actor-turned-screenwriter’s long-shot fight to get Rocky made.

ROCKY IS A work of fiction, but it’s fair to say Sylvester Stallone threw his heart and suffering onto the page. The then-29-year-old actor-turned-screenwriter was a Hollywood nobody when the boxing movie to end all boxing movies was filmed in early 1976 (with a release later that year). The now-80-year-old had done minor work in largely forgotten films (oh, and don’t forget the porno!) when he wrote himself his dream leading role and convinced studio United Artists to both make the film and take a chance on the hardscrabble, sometimes literally hard-to-understand Sly as the star.

This story is recounted in I Play Rocky, the acclaimed biopic about the making and myth behind both Rocky and Stallone, played by Anthony Ippolito. Sly is, alas, “all but indivisible” from his creation, as The Guardian wrote in a review of his new memoir The Steps, “each an extension of the other.” Sly has his own version of his ascension, though it’s laced with frustration toward family and a certain producer on Rocky who he feels fleeced him (more on that below).

But what’s real in I Play Rocky, what’s Hollywood-ified, and what’s Stallone’s own hard-won truth? Here we dig into the facts behind Rocky’s development, production, and eventual gangbusters box office reception. But we also get into Stallone’s life and career, where the two merge with Rocky “The Italian Stallion” Balboa, and how well I Play Rocky streamlines it all into popcorn fun.

Sylvester Stallone was born on July 6, 1946, in Hell’s Kitchen, then a rough neighborhood of Manhattan, according to History. As Sly tells it in a (fascinating) 1976 profile in The New York Times, he was raised by a “bickering Italian couple” who put him in foster care while they worked. (His hairdresser father, Francesco “Frank” Stallone Sr., who had a tiny part in Rocky as the timekeeper in the climax fight, is embodied by a curmudgeonly Matt Dillon in I Play Rocky. Stallone’s mother, Jacqueline “Jackie” Stallone, is not depicted, but had a wild career as an astrologer, trapeze artist, chorus girl, women’s-only gym owner, and boxing promoter.)

Stallone became a juvenile delinquent who “attended 12 schools by the time he was 15, and was kicked out of most of them.” More promisingly, the native New Yorker went to high school in Philadelphia, aka Rocky town, and threw himself into sports, being a star fullback and discus thrower. In an unexpected move, he then attended university at American College in Leysin, Switzerland, where he picked up a part-time job chasing men away from female dorms, except he found it was more lucrative to “look the other way” for two francs an hour (money that scored him flights back home).

Studying drama came next at the University of Miami for two years before he moved back to New York with the loftiest thespian ambitions. Instead, he found work as an usher at a movie theater and cleaning cages at a zoo. I Play Rocky starts with a very broke Stallone as a theater usher, though there’s no zoo action, and the story cuts the very funny fact that he was fired from said theater when he tried scalping a M*A*S*H ticket to the theater’s owner, Walter Reade. (Also absent from I Play Rocky: Among Sly’s ambitions was a fully autobiographical film that he planned to call From Roaches to Riches.)

Sly took what scraps he could in his New York days, appearing in the low-budget greaser comedy The Lords of Flatbush (contrary to I Play Rocky, he was a co-lead actor, and even wrote additional dialogue). He had an uncredited bit part in Robert Altman’s 1970 touchstone M*A*S*H (yes, the same film for which he tried to scalp a ticket) and acted in Capone (1975) as well as the Roger Corman-produced cult B-movie Death Race 2000 (1975), playing Machine Gun Joe Viterbo.

That’s not all. In desperate need of money, the real-life Italian Stallion took a part in the 1970 softcore porn film The Party at Kitty and Stud's, in which he lets it all hang out—without hardcore sex. He thought the movie was garbage, but he was paid $200 for two days of work. “It was either do that movie or rob someone because I was at the end—at the very end—of my rope,” Stallone told Playboy in 1978, according to Far Out.

California came calling. With the tiniest bit of fame to his name, he moved to Los Angeles with his first wife Sasha Czack (AnnaSophia Robb in I Play Rocky), where they lived in a one-and-a-half-bedroom apartment ''in the pancreas of Hollywood,” he told the Times, for $215 a month.

“Things weren’t going so well there,” Stallone said in an archival interview quoted by Forbes. “As a matter of fact, I actually had to go out and try to sell my dog because it was either that or he wasn’t going to be very well fed around the house.” In I Play Rocky, you see Stallone actually sell his bull mastiff Butkus—then locate and buy back Butkus, who would go on to be the dog in Rocky—though it’s hard to verify if things unfolded exactly this way.

Inspiration came when he watched the championship fight in 1975 between Chuck Wepner, a club fighter known as ''The Bayonne Bleeder,'' and world champion Muhammad Ali. “And for one brief moment, this supposed stumblebum turned out to be magnificent,” Stallone later mused, according to Forbes. “I thought if this isn’t a metaphor for life.”

The lore is that based on this brief moment, Stallone went on a tear, writing the script for Rocky in just three and a half days. This becomes a crucial montage in I Play Rocky, with Sly putting pen to paper, then snoozing while his wife types it out. In reality, Stallone told the Times that he had the fight in his mind for a month, “my inspiration stage. Then I let it incubate for 10 months, the incubation stage.” Finally, writing the screenplay in a mad dash was merely “the verification stage.” Stallone loves stages.

Much of the tension in I Play Rocky actually takes place before a frame of Rocky is shot. Stallone gets a meeting with two producers, Irwin Winkler (P.J. Byrne) and Robert Chartoff (Toby Kebbell). When he turns out not to be right for a part, on his way out of the office, he sneaks his Rocky script onto the secretary’s desk. In reality, Stallone had already sold several scripts, mostly to television, and he simply brought up the Rocky idea to the producers, who asked to see the script.

Winkler and Chartoff, playing up much of the comedic antics and sarcasm in I Play Rocky, loved Stallone’s screenplay. They just didn’t want him to play the title role. The producers were contracted with United Artists. The top brass threw out star names like Burt Reynolds, James Caan, and Ryan O’Neal. But Sly refused to sell the script unless he took the lead role. And refused again. Despite the fact that he had no car and $106 in the bank.

In I Play Rocky, the figure offered to buy the script on the condition that Stallone will not play Rocky goes up to an astronomical $360,000 (which in today’s money would be $2.1 million); however, the 1976 Times profile reports that bidding went up to $265,000. Either way, a beautiful heap of money. Finally, the producers and studio greenlit Rocky with a $1 million budget and paid Stallone $35,000 plus his acting fee. Stallone was Rocky Balboa. The entire production lasted 28 days, ''the gestation time for a water bug,'' Sly quipped to the Times.

Here’s the more important part of the contract that’s left out of I Play Rocky: Stallone sold the rights to Rocky and its characters in accepting the deal. Those rights went to Winkler—which has given Winkler a fortune plus power over the Rocky franchise, and fueled an ongoing feud between the 95-year-old producer and Stallone, who’s not shy about badmouthing Winkler. Stallone is adamant that he was swindled. Per Collider, he has called Winkler “nefarious” and “the remarkably untalented and parasitical producer of Rocky and Creed.”

Despite this supposed crooked deal, Stallone came out more than fine. What’s also not in I Play Rocky is that the then-unknown received 10 percent of the net profits (known as net points in the industry) of Rocky off the backend. Given that Rocky earned roughly $200 million at the box office, becoming the top hit of 1976—on top of picking up 10 Oscar nominations and an illustrious run in ancillary business—Stallone easily made millions off the original movie. (He claims $2.5 million, Winkler claims much higher.) He is leaps and leaps richer now.

Many forget that upon release, the critical response to Rocky was mixed, split between pans and raves. But it energized the masses, and its classic status is unquestionable now. In real life and I Play Rocky, Stallone comes out with a smile on his face, aware that his and his character’s rise from forgotten bum to underdog sensation is complete.

Are you a fan of Rocky? (If you’re not, how the hell are you reading this article?) How about Rocky II, Rocky III, the Creed movies? If so, yes, yes, yes, and again yes. On the other hand, if you don’t like Hollywood behind-the-scenes tales, boxing, or Rocky, sit this one out.

Though it fudges some turns of events and details, smoothing out the messiness and politics of a young star making his way in Hollywood, its insights can be revelatory—for example, the incredible contribution of Steadicam inventor Garrett Brown (played by real-life camera operator Michael Fuchs), whose experimental invention not only made the original Rocky possible on its shoestring budget and tight schedule, but brought a distinctive graceful movement to Rocky’s training and fighting scenes. The cast is all-around captivating; Ippolito finds soul in Stallone while managing a difficult and eccentric accent.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, as directed by Peter Farrelly (Green Book), I Play Rocky is also on the schmaltzy side. But when Sly, or Ippolito, sprints up those Philadelphia Art Museum steps determined to change history, your heart will do a little jump for him.

#4572. BYD now has 1.02 million workers, more than Toyota, GM, Ford, and Tesla combined

BYD now has more than 1.02 million employees, according to chairman Wang Chuanfu. That’s more people than Toyota, GM, Ford, and Tesla employ combined.

And it’s a big jump from the start of the year. BYD reported about 869,600 employees at the end of 2025, which means the Chinese automaker has added roughly 150,000 people in 10 months while its vehicle sales are down.

Roughly 960,000 of BYD’s people work in China and about 60,000 work abroad. Up to 120,000 of them are R&D engineers, according to Wang, who shared the figures on stage Wednesday at the China Society of Automotive Engineers’ (CSAE) 33rd annual conference. Their work covers battery cells, motors, electronic controls, and semiconductors.

Wang credits vertical integration for that scale. In his telling, keeping batteries, chips, and motors in-house is what took BYD from a battery maker founded in 1994 to the world’s top-selling new energy vehicle brand several years running. He called the company’s rise a microcosm of China’s auto industry going from follower to leader.

BYD’s workforce has been all over the place in the last few years.

The company had about 570,100 employees at the end of 2022 and 703,500 at the end of 2023. Then it went on a hiring spree. We reported in September 2024 that BYD had passed 900,000 employees and claimed the largest R&D workforce of any automaker, with over 110,000 engineers. It ended 2024 with 968,900 people.

Then came the first big cut. BYD’s 2025 annual report showed roughly 869,600 employees at year-end, a drop of about 99,000, mostly in frontline production jobs.

Now it’s back over a million. Data compiled by S&P Global Market Intelligence put BYD at 911,900 employees at the end of June, so the company added more than 100,000 people in about four months.

The gap with legacy automakers is massive. Volkswagen Group, which counts its Chinese joint ventures, reported 662,942 employees at the end of 2025. Toyota had 390,927 as of March 31, 2026, and Stellantis had 258,668 at the end of last year.

In the US, Ford ended 2025 with 169,000 employees and GM with 156,000. Tesla reported a worldwide headcount of 134,785 in its latest 10-K.

Add up Toyota, GM, Ford, and Tesla and you get about 851,000 people. BYD has roughly 170,000 more than that.

But headcount isn’t output. If you divide 2025 global vehicle sales by year-end workforce, BYD comes out far behind:

BYD sold about 4.6 million vehicles last year with 869,600 employees, or 5.3 vehicles per worker. Tesla delivered 1,636,129 vehicles with 134,785 people, about 12 per worker, and Volkswagen Group was at about 13.5. Toyota, with 11.3 million group sales including Daihatsu and Hino, got roughly 29 vehicles out of each employee.

There’s a catch, and it’s a big one. BYD’s headcount isn’t only a car company’s headcount. It includes BYD Electronic, its majority-owned contract manufacturer that assembles devices for other brands and reported 165,000 employees of its own at the end of 2025. It also covers BYD’s battery business, which supplies other automakers, plus its in-house chips, motors, energy storage, and rail transit operations.

In short, BYD’s vertical integration largely drives its high headcount.

BYD sold 3,131,576 vehicles in the first nine months of 2026, down 3.9% year-over-year. September was its best month of the year at 463,561 units, but the company has been stuck in a brutal price war at home and is losing ground to rivals like Geely and Leapmotor. Its first-half revenue (344.8 billion yuan) and net profit (12.3 billion yuan) were both down year-over-year.

All of the growth is overseas. BYD’s international sales hit 1,342,960 units through September, up 92.7%, and they now make up about 43% of its total volume. That’s on top of BYD beating Tesla on pure EV deliveries again in Q2.

Yet only 60,000 of its 1.02 million workers are based outside China. That’s about 6%. So BYD is still building nearly everything at home and shipping it out, even as its factories in Thailand, Brazil, and Hungary come online.

The 1.02 million number makes for a great headline, but we wouldn’t read it as a sign of strength on its own.

BYD doesn't just make cars. It makes a lot of battery and other parts that go into other things such as other automaker's EVs.

It is automakers, auto supplier, battery makers, electronic contract manufacturer all merged into one.

Remember GM used to make refrigerators and satellites in addition to cars at one point.

BYD’s whole model is to make almost everything itself: cells, chips, motors, seats, and a lot more. That’s a big reason it can sell a Seagull for around $10,000 in China and still make money. But it’s a labor-heavy model, and it works because Chinese factory labor is relatively cheap and plentiful. Toyota gets more than five times as many cars out of each employee. Tesla gets more than twice as many.

The problem is that BYD’s growth is now outside China, and that’s where this model gets tested. Only 6% of its workforce is abroad, yet 43% of its sales are. Tariffs in Europe, Brazil, Mexico, and elsewhere are pushing BYD to build locally, but a factory in Hungary or Brazil won’t necessarily produce the same.

The number that should worry legacy automakers is the 120,000 engineers. That’s almost as many people as Tesla employs in total, all working on product.

#4571. Face-to-Face Meetings in Surrogacy Can Change So Much

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 7, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

There has been a lot of discussion in the news recently about problematic surrogacy relationships, and some that have been highly problematic. One of the tools I have used and presented at the annual conference of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine is a way to reframe the surrogacy contract with your gestational carrier, before you start the process, to help ensure everyone’s values are aligned. You can read more here.

Another tool I have used, which is often suggested but easily dismissed, is a weekly face-to-face call between the gestational carrier and the intended parents. To see why this can be so important, let’s first look at the relationship between the intended parents and gestational carrier and how it evolves during the journey.

Many intended parents and gestational carriers feel like they are “in love” with each other from the beginning. Yet this feeling can be deceiving. Beneath it is often a gestational carrier who sees herself as a giver or a helper, doing something incredibly valuable and, in doing so, fulfilling her desire to help others. The result is a wonderful feeling for her and reinforcement of her self-esteem. The intended parents have often been waiting a long time and are deeply grateful to this person who will help them achieve their dream. It is a win-win for everyone.

These feelings may increase with the busy pace of doctor's appointments, meetings, and legal requirements. They are on a roller coaster of joy and good feelings. Yet they don’t have any history together or a foundation for their relationship.

They may have a Zoom or FaceTime call from time to time but eventually decide to let the relationship grow “organically,” which usually translates into a texting relationship with calls and perhaps visits for milestone appointments. This arrangement may be fine and can work for many people. However, once the excitement fades and the gestational carrier's pregnancy is stable, the doctor’s appointments lessen and everyone feels free to go back to reengaging with their lives more. Perhaps the gestational carrier feels she can catch up on work or spend more time with her children, and the intended parents feel free to take the time to focus on work or friends. Calls and texts may become less frequent, and everyone feels it is OK to coast. But is it?

At this point, the fetus no longer looks like a piece of rice on the ultrasound, and the intended parents may feel fine having a little more free time at first, but after a while they may start to feel out of control. They see the images and consider that their baby is growing in someone else’s body, perhaps miles away. They may start to feel anxious and out of control, and without realizing it, they may begin to micromanage the gestational carrier or worry about what she is eating or doing.

At the same time, the gestational carrier, who was feeling so much love, admiration, and attention from the intended parents, may now realize that while she is getting calls after her doctor’s appointments, she's getting fewer about her husband’s new job or son’s Little League tryout. She may start to feel objectified without realizing it.

Without knowing it, both parties can sense a growing distance between them, and if something goes wrong at this time, they may feel less willing to step outside of themselves to consider the other's position. Remember, it is much easier to have a heart-to-heart discussion with someone you are close to than with someone you are not as close to.

Now let’s consider what a weekly face-to-face meeting can do to change this scenario. Consider a time at work when you meet a new employee. Maybe that person is someone you think you will be close friends with or not, but you see them regularly. You see them in the washroom, the holiday party, and in the hallway. Eventually, you sit down next to this person at a meeting, and you feel comfortable in their presence. Why? Because your brain registered this person as familiar and safe. Face-to-face interactions tell your body you can trust this person. Texting cannot create this experience.

So, while it may seem forced in the beginning to set up these weekly Zoom or FaceTime meetings, they can pay off in spades. They don’t need to be serious. They can be short and simple. Just talking about what you are meal prepping for the week, what you are watching on Netflix, or how your dog training is going works. Through these calls, you are building the bricks of a foundation that will carry you through the pregnancy. Then, when the gestational carrier's doctor tells her that the pregnancy is stable and the appointments lessen, everyone has a solid bond.

On the surface, it is easy to see how these weekly face-to-face meetings can create a warm and friendly relationship, making the journey better for everyone and helping create memories that you can document and share with your child (see my Lifebook for more information). But your foundation can also help shield you against problems that may unexpectedly surface. So, while it may seem like a bit of an imposition at first, in the long term, this face-to-face contact can pay off in enormous ways.

#4570. Is Yeti’s $200 Camp Blanket Worth It? I Tested It Out for Months to Find Out.

Hint: It low-key might be one of Yeti’s best products.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

YETI IS KNOWN to drop a lot of product. The Austin-based brand emerged as a key player in the cooler category and has since grown immensely, putting out everything from fleeces to outdoor furniture.

The Lowlands Blanket, an durable outdoor blanket, might be a piece that gets overlooked in the brand’s offering. The original came out a few years back but Yeti has added some new colors as well as improvements like the diamond-stitched pattern. It’s waterproof, claims to repel dirt and pet hair, and comes in a host of core and seasonal colors (not to mention two different sizes). As an all-purpose, throw-kind of blanket, it’s meant to be put to use pretty much anywhere, from the back of your car or atop some cold bleachers at the soccer game to the campsite or picnic at the beach or state park.

Do you need one though? That all depends. The $200 blanket proved quite capable during testing, packing down nicely and drying at speed. There are pros and cons to the thing, and it really depends on the lifestyle you’re trying to cater to, not to mention the elements you might be operating under.

While we were sitting on a regular-sized Lowlands Blanket during the summer months (quite literally), packing it to a few outdoor concerts and park picnics, we mostly waited patiently for fall. We wanted to really assess the burly, insulated build of the thing and its waterproofness. We spent several weeks with the blanket in the back of the car, at the ready for everything from dog naps and post-paddle warmups to hangouts near the wet soccer field or full-fledged fall camping trips.

Right out of the gate, this is easily one of the most comfortable outdoor blankets we’ve tested in recent history. Down blankets can offer a similar level of sensory joy but the softness of the topside of this blanket feels like something you’d get draped over the best chair in a ski lodge, right in front of the great room fire. It’s mildly fuzzy on one side and more coarse and rugged on the other.

The seasonal colors really pop and add some flavor while the two sizes of the blanket are actually quite distinct and useful in their own ways. The smaller, about 28-in. by 38-in., is about the size of a dog bed and is (surprise) best for pets—setting up a dry sitting spot for one, or thawing wipe downs after playing in the snow. It does not come with a carrying case but rolls up plenty small and doesn’t necessitate one. The larger (the one we tested), measuring 55-in. by 78-in., is more like a bed topper, great for picnics, topping your camp bed, or just wearing around in the cold.

The corner loops are a nice touch for securing the blanket in blustery conditions and can also be used for hanging or tying down valuables. We even tried hanging it up and utilizing it as a temporary wind barrier during outings that involved occasional sideways rain. We found that it worked well as a barrier during offseason camping trips. In other words, as a comforter of sorts to protect you from dirt or the elements while keeping your base-layers or sheets beneath dry.

Cleaning the thing is pretty simple, whether that be a quick wipe-down to address grass stains and mud or a full machine wash after a weekend camping in the woods. One of the blanket’s biggest merits is its thickness, offering more depth than most at close to a half-inch. You can genuinely feel it too. Often, when you throw a packable blanket atop the grass or the sand at the beach you’re banking on the inherent softness of that natural surface and not getting much else. Not so with the Yeti, as it does afford a true layer of added comfort, one that can easily eat up contours in uneven surfaces or small rocks and sticks.

Yeti tends to follow the go big or go home philosophy, which we’re used to at this point and oftentimes suits the product and its intentions well. At nearly six pounds, it’s admittedly a bit heavy for a blanket. But you can feel instantly where all that weight is going (the ample insulation and reinforced exterior). The weight is not a huge deal, especially if you utilize the packing bag that it comes with, which you can grab by hand or sling over your shoulder. It’s more noticeable if you’re just carrying it about unfolded or rearranging that picnic spread. But, because it translates to more comfort and durability, we’re all for it. Just keep it in mind for towing purposes if you’re looking for something to pack along on a hike, you can find something far lighter.

The internet has alerted us to the possibility of mold if not dried off properly or machine-washed fairly often. While we didn’t experience that, the blanket is thicker and seemingly takes on odors a bit more than some. What’s perhaps more of an issue is the noise, which is only relatively louder than, say, a puffy blanket, which tends to offer a more whispered kind of sound when moving about beneath it. This is probably only a real issue for sensitive sleepers.

For do-it-all blankets built for the outdoors, there are a few alternatives. Rumpl has a line of nimble options that often come in cool patterns. The price is right but you’re generally getting either a mat or a puffy (although you can certainly pair the two up for more waterproofness). They’re billed as weather-resistant and while they look great and feel like snuggling into a zipped sleeping bag, they don’t quite have the waterproof build and toughness of Yeti. However, if you’re after a high warmth-to-weight ratio, it’s tough to go wrong here. Nomadix makes another quality option, a puffer blanket that packs more tightly than most, weighs just two pounds, and is even made with a bunch of recycled material. Yet, if you’re going to be dealing with more than wet grass (e.g. snow) or plan to be in more than low-level precipitation, you’ll want something more substantial.

White Duck Outdoors makes a solid one too in the Trailside Blanket, which comes in under $100, weighs just three pounds, has a streamlined layer of insulation, and smart magnetic closures for when you want to wear it. While a lot of Pendleton’s blankets are form over function, the Oregon brand does make a nice all-weather option in the Roll-Up Blanket, priced comparably to the new Yeti. It does come armed with a weather-resistant nylon side and a soft wool side to hang out on.

For an all-purpose outdoor blanket that can take you from the snowy slopes to the trail and pretty much everywhere in between, this is a tough one to beat. It’s more durable than many we’ve tested, offers more comfort by way of added depth and nicely-stitched insulation, and even fends off pet hair swimmingly. While a great accompaniment to camping adventures, the Lowlands Blanket is also great for elevating the outdoor music festival, throwing atop a damp yard, or lugging to the tailgater (especially in the fall and winter).

This regular size is $200, a fair chunk of change (the small version is $75). And while that’s not cheap, it simply outdoes just about every other blanket in its class. You may not need a heavier, weatherproof blanket if you mostly spend time car camping. But if you want a burly blanket that’s not afraid of the terrain or weather, this one’s for you. Offseason campers are wise to consider it, as are diehard sports fans who like to show up for their team.

#4569. When one door closes: Polestar 2 production ends, and epic EV deals

Forget about the 600+ hp hybrid-powered Polestar 1 supercoupe; the car that established Polestar as a standalone brand was the 2. As the brand pulls out of the US and shifts its focus to the rest of the world, it’s time to look back at the EV that helped define Polestar, along with a look around at some of the best EV deals of all time.

A number of European news sites (including Electrive and TV2 Broom) are reporting that the last new Polestar 2 has rolled off the company’s Luqiao assembly line, with more than 200,000 of the all-electric sedan/hatchbacks built in China since the electric sedan launched in 2020. And, while the company hasn’t confirmed that with any sort of official announcement, the news jives with the company’s previously announced plans to release an updated Polestar 2 in 2027, followed by an all-new Polestar 7 SUV that’s set to follow in early 2028.

With the brand set to pull out of the US after the Trump Administration’s Commerce Department declined to grant it authorization under the Connected Vehicle Rule earlier this year, it might at first seem like that US Polestar fans will miss out on that freshened 2, whatever shape it takes – but don’t lose hope, yet.

First shown in 2016, the original Volvo Concept 40.2 was supposed to be a new, entry-level sedan for the now Geely-owned Volvo, which was in the process of separating itself from Ford ownership and the Focus-based C30 coupe and S40/V50 sedan and wagons. And a fine entry-level Volvo it would have been, too, if Tesla’s share price hadn’t made it worth more than the next five most valuable car companies combined.

See, once Tesla (or, more to the point, $TSLA) did that, every carmaker in the world figured the stock market would bless them with billions, too, and started announcing plans to go all electric, right now. Volvo parent company Geely, however, decided they’d fast-track the process, taking the next two Volvo models in their pipeline (the C90 coupe version of the S90 sedan and the C40 sedan previewed by the Concept 40.2) and made them Polestars.

A SPAC merger later, and Polestar was spun off as not only its own brand, but its own, largely Chinese-owned company – which brings us to where we are now.

In the US the Polestar 3 Long-Range Single Motor (RWD) SUV starts at something like $67,500 and offers a 111 kWh battery pack good for an EPA-rated range of up to 350 miles. The top-shelf Performance-spec Polestar 3, meanwhile, offers an all-wheel-drive dual-motor setup that Polestar rates at 380 kW (~517 hp) that will launch you across suburbia with a 0–60 mph time in the 4 second range, albeit with slightly less range than the base model … but that $67,500 price is really more of a suggestion these days.

Polestar is offering a $23,000 discount on the 3 and a $25,000, rebate, market adjustment or whatever on the 4. That means that you can get a brand new Polestar 3 or 4 with Chinese EV tech and more than a little bit of Volvo safety baked in for a dramatically reduced price. If you pick the right one at the right dealer, probably for less than $40,000.

One of the best looking cars from the last decade… the 2024+ RWD is such a great value…. I got one myself a year ago for $28k with 5k on the odometer.

As for the 2, I have a bit of a personal connection to that one. My son picked up a 19,000 mile 2024 Polestar 2 Long-Range Single Motor (RWD) in Glacier for under $22K, which is an absolutely shocking price for a fast, capable sporty sedan hatchback that isn’t just a worthy successor to the S40 it was meant to replace, but a solid foundation for an EV brand that got wrapped up in politics.

Check out the links below to see what kind of deal you can get on a new Polestar near you, and if you’re interested in a 2, you can probably score a great deal there, too. Let us know what you find in the comments.

#4568. New Trek e-bike is first to get Bosch’s new motor with a major power upgrade

Trek is getting a head start on the competition with the latest version of its Marlin+ electric mountain bike, becoming the first North American bicycle manufacturer to feature Bosch’s newly upgraded Active Line Plus motor.

The updated drive system brings more power, less weight, and a smaller footprint to Trek’s approachable electric mountain bike platform, helping make the Marlin+ 6 Gen 2 an even more compelling option for riders who want a capable e-bike without necessarily stepping up to a full-blown, high-performance electric mountain bike.

The Trek Marlin+ has traditionally occupied an interesting Goldilocks position in the company’s electric mountain bike lineup. It’s designed to offer the versatility of a trail-capable eMTB while remaining practical enough for everyday recreational riding, commuting, and exploring gravel paths.

In other words, it’s the kind of electric mountain bike that doesn’t require you to be an actual mountain biker to enjoy it.

And the new Bosch motor seems particularly well suited to that mission.

The biggest upgrade comes courtesy of Bosch’s new-generation Active Line Plus motor, which now offers up to 600 watts of power and 60 Nm of torque.

That’s paired with up to 340% pedal assistance, giving riders a substantial boost when accelerating or tackling climbs.

Despite the improved performance, Bosch has actually managed to shrink the motor. A redesigned two-stage gearbox reduces its volume by 17% while shaving approximately 1.1 lb (0.5 kg) from the previous generation.

The new motor weighs just around 6 lb (2.7 kg), helping manufacturers like Trek build lighter, more streamlined electric bicycles.

Bosch has also focused on improving the riding experience, with updated sensors and software designed to provide smoother, more natural-feeling assistance. Specially machined gears help make the motor virtually silent, while improved sealing and bearings are designed to withstand riding in all weather conditions.

The motor provides pedal assistance up to 20 mph (32 km/h) in the US, making it a Class 1 e-bike without a throttle. With a launch price of US $2,999, it’s also one of the more affordable options in Trek’s lineup.

For a bike like the Marlin+, that combination of moderate weight, smooth assistance, and plenty of usable power could be more important than chasing the enormous torque figures found on increasingly powerful premium eMTBs.

The new motor isn’t the only addition to Bosch’s electric bicycle ecosystem this fall.

The company has also unveiled its new Intuvia 200 display, featuring a 2.4-inch grayscale screen designed to remain readable in bright sunlight. It’s joined by a redesigned LED Controller that’s approximately 65% smaller than the previous LED Remote, offering five thumb-operated buttons and a USB-C charging port.

Bosch is also expanding its theft protection technology with an updated ConnectModule that uses Bluetooth Low Energy alongside GPS and cellular connectivity to help locate stolen e-bikes within a few yards, including in areas where GPS reception is poor.

Perhaps most interesting for long-distance riders is the new PowerTube 720 battery, which packs 720 Wh of capacity into a compact package weighing just 8.6 lb (3.9 kg). Bosch claims up to 115 miles (185 km) of range under favorable conditions on compatible touring e-bikes.

Those additional products are part of Bosch’s broader smart system updates, though Trek hasn’t confirmed which, if any, will be included on the updated Marlin+.

With Bosch supplying drive systems to a large number of e-bike makers worldwide, these upgrades will likely find their way onto plenty of other electric bicycles in the coming months.

But for now, Trek gets the distinction of being first in North America to bring the new Active Line Plus motor to riders.

#4567. We Need to Talk About Women and Social Anxiety

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 7, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

Consciousness-raising has its origins in the second-wave feminism of the 1960s, notably with the New York Radical Women, perhaps best known for staging a protest at the 1968 Miss America pageant. Feminist consciousness-raising aimed to help women realise that a lot of their problems were not individual, but instead resulted from institutional sexism—being caged by traditional gender roles is one example. A popular slogan of the time, "the personal is political," encapsulates the same sentiment, for it puts forth that oppression within domestic spheres (the home, family, and relationships) is not separate from wider power structures in society (gender inequality).

In 2026, we’re arguably in the age of post-feminism, where conventional wisdom often holds that the work of the women’s movement has been done.

While we’ve certainly come a long way, what came to the fore when I interviewed socially anxious women as part of my research (Masters, 2024) was that we still have some way to go. That is to say, a lot of these women’s experiences not only evoked sexism, but they described such experiences as being a key part of their social anxiety.

Ellen* described regularly enduring street harassment, and how this was central to her social anxiety: "[I]t constantly happens […] it’s an everyday battle, so therefore why would you not internalise […] take that with you and worry about it the next day?"

Ria* told me about making suggestions for improvements in work meetings, only for them to get ignored—except these same things were later implemented when male colleagues brought them up. She spoke about the effect this had on her self-confidence, adding, "[W]hen it happens more than once […] eventually, it’s going to chip away at you, isn’t it?"

These experiences are "everyday," but they’re underpinned by bigger issues: Think about Ria’s being undermined in the workplace and the gender pay gap—6.8 percent in 2026 (Office for National Statistics, 2026)—or Ellen’s street harassment and sexual violence—1 in 4 women over the age of 16 in England and Wales has been raped or sexually assaulted (ONS, 2025). (For examples of even more overt and, frankly, frightening misogynistic experiences, see Laura Bates’s Everyday Sexism Project.)

Ellen’s and Ria’s experiences could be characterised as more subtle nods to sexism, sometimes so subtle that those to whom they happen might question whether they’re being too sensitive. Another woman I interviewed, Farah, told me that when she would openly decry occurrences such as these, people would often respond to her by saying "Well, you’re so sensitive."

This only stokes social anxiety further: In particular, it promotes what psychologist Gillian Butler dubs the "post-mortem" of events (2016). We might think, "Did I get offended too easily? Was it my fault? What if I deserved it? Was it even as bad as I thought? Was I just imagining it? Why is no one else speaking up?"

Professor of Counselling Psychology Derald Wing Sue calls events like those described above "microaggressions" (2010). Crucially, Sue says that when these happen to us, we search for patterns in terms of similar past experiences. In so doing, we often see a link between these experiences and an aspect of our identity: being a woman, being from an ethnic minority, or being disabled, to name but a few.

The very nature of social anxiety is a fear of being negatively evaluated, and for this fear to exist at all, we need to believe that such negative evaluation is warranted. And it wouldn’t be warranted unless we perceive ourselves to be not good enough, or odd, or bad in some way—not like everybody else. So, as I’ve argued elsewhere (Masters, 2024), it’s possible that socially anxious women attribute these events not to their identities, but to themselves, as individuals.

Given this, it can be very heartening to learn that, actually, some of these experiences are like everybody else’s: They don't just happen to us. I’m not talking about a type of schadenfreude, or taking pleasure in another’s misfortune, but rather, realising that we’re not alone in these experiences, in feeling angry about them, or in feeling more socially anxious in light of them. It’s not us that’s at fault, and the way we feel—frustrated, afraid of being judged, lacking in confidence—is quite understandable.

Perhaps the most straightforward way to have these kinds of revelations is by talking to others. It still does feel a bit taboo, doesn’t it, talking openly about sexism, like you might just be dismissed as "moaning" or told that women have it so good now, or that our perceived injustices are down to our personal choices. But if we don’t talk about it, we’ll never have an appreciation that these things are happening to other women too—and, often, they feel much the same way as we do.

"Talking about it" doesn’t need to be a formal undertaking: You don’t need to set up a monthly consciousness-raising group in your neighbourhood for fellow socially anxious women. But, hey, if you want to, go right ahead—and let me know when and where it is so I can come!

Of course, "talking" on its own isn’t going to change long-entrenched societal structures and injustices overnight, but it’s certainly a start. The New York Radical Women themselves had humble beginnings: At the outset, they were just five in number, and met regularly in members’ apartments across Manhattan. It might be as simple as asking a friend, "Hey, has this ever happened to you?" or "Do you ever feel like…?"

Activist Judi Chamberlin talks about the importance of consciousness-raising not in terms of feminism, but for those experiencing mental distress. She says it "helps people to see that their so-called symptoms are indications of real problems […] Instead of believing that they have a defect in their psychic makeup (or neurochemical system), participants learn to recognize the oppressive conditions in their daily lives."

Consciousness-raising can thus provide the means with which to push back against some of the beliefs on which social anxiety thrives: that we’re odd or different; that these things happen only to us; and that we’re to blame for both the occurrences themselves and the social anxiety that’s intertwined with them.

I want to end on some words by novelist Alice Walker, for she encapsulates the potential power of consciousness-raising rather well in writing that we must "resist the temptation to think what afflicts you is peculiar to you. Have faith that what is in your consciousness can be communicated to the consciousness of all. And is, in many cases, already there (1989).

Bates, Laura. (n.d.). Everyday Sexism Project

Butler, Gillian. (2016). Overcoming Social Anxiety and Shyness: A self-help guide using cognitive behavioural techniques. 2nd edition. London: Robinson.

Chamberlin, Judi. (2012 [1977]). On Our Own: Patient-controlled Alternatives to the Mental Health System. Lawrence, Massachusetts: National Empowerment Centre, Inc.

Masters, Katie. (2024). Feminist and Anti-psychiatry Perspectives on ‘Social Anxiety Disorder’: The Socially Anxious Woman. Cham: Palgrave Macmillan.

Office for National Statistics. (2026). Gender pay gap in the UK: 2026

Office for National Statistics. (2025). Sexual offences prevalence and victim characteristics, England and Wales

Sue, Derald Wing. (2010). Microaggressions in Everyday Life: Race, Gender, and Sexual Orientation. John Wiley and Sons.

Walker, Alice. (1989). The Temple of My Familiar. San Diego: Harcourt Brace Jovanovich.

#4566. Here Are the 7 Best Long-Sleeve Shirts for Cold-Weather Workouts

Stay dry, cool, and protected during your workouts with our favorite long-sleeve shirts.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

FALL IS HERE, and with it, the chill is starting to hit the air. This change in temperature shifts the spotlight to what we think is the unsung hero of your fall and winter workout wardrobe, especially when it comes to your workouts: the long-sleeve T-shirt.

Whether you’re trying to ward off goosebumps or protect your skin from the sun, long-sleeve shirts are a solid choice for training. Many are made from the same performance fabrics as our favorite workout shirts; they can wick moisture and keep you cooler than a wool layer while offering more coverage than a short-sleeve tee.

Collectively, the Men’s Health editorial team has trained in dozens of long-sleeve shirts and pooled our experience to bring you seven picks for different types of training.

The long-sleeve sibling of our best overall workout shirt also snags the top spot in our roundup of long-sleeve workout shirts. After all, it’s virtually the same shirt, just better suited for fall and winter workouts.

The Strato Tech Tee is among the softest shirts I’ve ever worn, and after a year of consistent use, mine still looks, feels, and performs much like it did during my first week of testing. Its four-way-stretch fabric contributes to its excellent comfort, and despite the shirt’s paper-thin feel, it was surprisingly effective at wicking moisture during our sweatiest workouts.

Because it’s lightweight, keeps sweat at bay, and is versatile enough to double as an everyday shirt, the Strato Tech earns its near-$70 price tag. It’s the kind of staple worth investing in.

The skin-tight fit of compression gear doesn’t appeal to everyone, but compression shirts offer plenty of utility. You can wear one on its own, under a short-sleeve tee for a fall or winter workout, or as a base layer for skiing and hiking.

Dick’s Sporting Goods’ DSG compression crew is a good option for skeptical buyers. It costs $30 per shirt and comes in more than 15 color options. The trade-off for that affordability is slightly less comfort. In particular, the seams that run along the arms can be a little annoying. It also runs a bit longer than I prefer, so I opted to tuck mine in.

Read More: Best Compression Shirts, Tested by Us

Gymshark has cemented itself as a major player in the fitness apparel space, not just because of the quality of its clothing, but also because its marketing and product lines often reflect what the current generation of gymgoers are wearing.

The Power Long Sleeve T-Shirt is a good example. It leans into the current pump-cover trend, where lifters wear oversized layers at the start of a workout and shed them once they’re warmed up and pumped. The Power Tee fits oversized but true to size and keeps the look simple, save for “Gymshark” printed across the back. It also comes in four colors.

Because it’s made from 95% cotton, expect it to hold onto more heat and sweat than a technical training shirt. I wouldn’t reach for it for hard runs or conditioning sessions, but for lifting, it works well either as a standalone shirt or as an extra layer to keep you warm between sets.

When people think of Under Armour, they often think of compression gear, so its HeatGear line—a collection designed to provide coverage while keeping athletes cool—is a natural pick for anyone who wants to keep their arms covered during spring and summer workouts.

Athletes who wear pads, trail runners looking for protection from brush, and even people with sun-sensitive skin can all benefit from the extra coverage. HeatGear fabric is ventilated and described by Under Armour as “ultra-light,” so the shirt offers protection without adding much bulk or warmth. And at $40 with 16 color options, it’s an affordable, versatile choice that works as either a standalone training shirt or a base layer.

Co-owned by Mark Wahlberg, Municipal is a lifestyle and fitness brand that makes gear for activities including training, golf, and running. The Enduro Stretch LS can work as a running shirt, but its minimal branding and simple design make it versatile enough for lifting, errands, or casual wear, too.

It has the hallmarks of a solid workout shirt: super stretch, moisture-wicking fabric, and a lightweight feel, all from a 100% polyester construction. The ribbed cuffs bring a lot more durability to the sleeves and a little style, so that you get more use out of this piece.

Municipal is still a relatively young brand, and the Enduro Stretch LS is only available in three colors, with fewer customer reviews than some of the more established options on this list. At this price, that makes it a slightly less proven pick, but its simple design and performance-focused construction give it plenty of appeal for runners and lifters alike.

If most of your training takes place outside, this is the shirt worth investing in. Ten Thousand—a brand that’s made it onto our best workout shirt and best workout shorts lists—built the Tactical Long Sleeve with sun protection, odor-blocking technology, and micro-mesh fabric designed to help regulate body temperature.

The shirt also uses flatlock seams, which lie flatter against the skin and help reduce irritation while reinforcing high-stress areas. The upper back, or yoke, is reinforced to better withstand ruck sacks, plate carriers, and weighted vests. There are a few trade-offs: It only comes in two colors (black and green), the care instructions are a little finicky, and it costs close to $100.

The Tactical is one of those buy-once, cry-once purchases that cost more up front but may save you money if it holds up longer than cheaper shirts. And Ten Thousand does have a one-year guarantee on their clothes. That said, not everyone wants to—or can— spend that much on a workout shirt, and you certainly don’t need one this rugged for every outdoor training session.

If you like wearing sleeves year-round, it’s worth investing in a lightweight shirt that keeps you covered without trapping too much heat. Barbell Apparel’s Arid Drop Hem Long Sleeve is made from a blend of bamboo, polyester, and a touch of spandex for added stretch and mobility. Customers describe it as lightweight and flattering, which tracks for a brand that built its name making clothes for people with more athletic builds.

Designed for warm-weather use, the Arid also includes odor control and UV protection, while its looser fit through the torso helps keep the fabric from clinging as you sweat. Aesthetically, it fits in just about anywhere, and its two neutral color options—black and a grayish blue—make it easier to get more mileage out of the hefty price tag.

Most workout shirts are made primarily from synthetic materials such as polyester, nylon, and elastane. These fabrics tend to dry faster than cotton and can be engineered to move moisture away from your skin, which helps keep the shirt from feeling soaked during a workout.

Cotton, by comparison, absorbs and holds onto more moisture, which can leave a shirt feeling heavy and damp and may contribute to chafing or irritation. That doesn’t mean cotton has no place in workout gear. Some shirts blend in a small amount to soften the fabric and improve comfort. An all-cotton shirt may be less appealing for sweaty sessions, but a little cotton in the blend isn’t necessarily a drawback.

Odor control generally comes down to two things: how quickly the fabric dries and whether it has been treated to limit odor-causing bacteria. Moisture-wicking, quick-drying fabrics can help keep sweat from sitting against your skin for as long, but the fabric itself doesn’t automatically prevent odor.

Some manufacturers also treat fibers with antimicrobial technologies designed to slow bacterial growth. Silver, copper, and zinc-based treatments are common examples. Other brands use different chemical or bio-based treatments to achieve a similar effect. If odor control matters to you, look for a specific antimicrobial or anti-odor claim rather than assuming every synthetic shirt has it.

You probably don’t need to obsess over seams, but they’re worth paying attention to if you’re prone to chafing. Look for flatlock seams, which sit flatter and feel less bulky against the skin, as well as thoughtful seam placement in high-friction areas.

The armpit is one of the more annoying places to have bulky stitching, which is why some workout shirts use raglan sleeves. Instead of a traditional sleeve seam that starts at the shoulder, raglan sleeves extend up toward the collar and create diagonal seams across the upper chest and back. That construction can reduce irritation and allow for more freedom of movement.

No. Many long-sleeve workout shirts are lightweight enough to wear comfortably during spring and summer, depending on the temperature and your personal preference.

There are also practical reasons to cover up in warm weather. Long sleeves can help shield your arms from direct sun and offer some protection from rough brush, branches, gravel, and other elements if you train outdoors or spend a lot of time on the trails.

As a fitness writer, personal trainer, and guy who likes to train, I spend a lot of time in workout clothes, usually while lifting or running. I’m fortunate that companies send me samples throughout the year—always with no strings attached—to test, and Men’s Health will occasionally ship specific products to my house for dedicated testing.

Creating this list was a collective effort between the Men’s Health editorial team and me, including Fitness and Reviews Editor Charles Thorp, NASM, Fitness Director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S., and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan. Our standard testing protocol is to wear each shirt for at least two weeks and put it through common exercises like pull-ups, push-ups, and deadlifts. At the time I wrote this article, I was also logging 15 to 25 miles of running per week across the treadmill, road, and local trails, so I rotated several of these shirts through those sessions to see how they held up.

We take notes on each shirt’s style, fit, comfort, price, versatility, and performance, including stretch, moisture management, and breathability. We also pay attention to sizing—whether a shirt fits true to size or runs large or small—and how the fabric holds up after repeated workouts and washes. What we don’t do is chase trends. Our goal is to recommend shirts that perform well now and should still make sense years from now.

Andrew Gutman, NASM-CPT is a journalist with a decade of experience covering fitness and nutrition. His work has been published in Men's Health, Men's Journal, Muscle & Fitness, and Gear Patrol. Outside of writing, Andrew trains in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, helps coach his gym's kickboxing team, and enjoys reading and cooking.

Charles Thorp is the Fitness and Reviews Editor at Men’s Health, where he shares the best product recommendations in gym equipment, recovery tools, supplements, and more. Following an early life in athletics, Charles became a NASM-certified trainer and began writing programs alongside the most respected coaches in the world.   Since entering the world of fitness content, Charles has had the opportunity to learn from and train alongside high performance individuals from the NFL, UFC, NBA, Formula 1, CrossFit, US Olympics, and Navy SEALs. When he’s not writing about training programs or gear, he can be seen at the gym or in the wild, putting them to the test.

#4565. BYD (BYDDY) Q3 profit jumps 28% on exports, but inventory balloons 60%

BYD’s Q3 2026 earnings are out, and net profit jumped 28% year-over-year to ¥10.02 billion as the Chinese automaker shipped more than half a million vehicles out of the country in just three months.

But the rest of the filing is messier. BYD’s inventory is up 60% since January, its cash pile has shrunk by almost half, and profit is still down for the first nine months of the year.

BYD is still operating at a high level, but its business is changing.

BYD filed its third-quarter report with the Hong Kong Stock Exchange on Thursday. Here are the key figures for July through September:

That’s BYD’s best quarterly profit since the end of 2024, and the first time revenue has grown year-over-year after four straight quarters of declines.

It’s also a big rebound from the start of the year. BYD’s Q1 2026 profit collapsed 55% to ¥4.08 billion, before recovering to ¥8.24 billion in Q2.

Still, it came in under expectations. Brokerages polled by Reuters were looking for ¥11.4 billion to ¥12.95 billion.

And zoom out to the full year so far, and BYD is treading water. Revenue for the first nine months was ¥566.30 billion, up just 0.01%, while net profit fell 4.2% to ¥22.34 billion. That’s on top of 2025, when BYD’s annual profit had already dropped to ¥32.62 billion from ¥40.25 billion in 2024.

The quarterly report doesn’t break out vehicle volumes, but BYD’s monthly sales filings do. The automaker sold 1,323,065 vehicles in Q3, up 18.7% from 1,114,192 a year earlier.

All of that growth, and then some, came from outside China. BYD exported 550,704 vehicles in the quarter, up 137% from 232,806 in Q3 2025. Everything else, which is mostly the Chinese market, fell about 12% to roughly 772,000 units.

Exports now account for 42% of BYD’s sales. In the first half, overseas markets already brought in ¥181.3 billion, or 53% of the company’s revenue.

For perspective, Tesla delivered 486,532 vehicles worldwide in Q3. BYD exported more cars than Tesla sold on the entire planet.

At home, it’s a different story. China’s price war hasn’t let up, and BYD is now fighting it with cars like the new Seagull with 5-minute flash charging, starting under $10,000. That’s great for buyers. Not so much for margins.

BYD doesn’t report gross margin in its quarterly filing, but it can be calculated from the income statement. We get about 18.0% for Q3, slightly better than 17.6% a year ago, but down from roughly 18.9% in Q2.

The bigger hits are further down the income statement.

Finance expenses came in at ¥7.37 billion for the first nine months, compared to a ¥2.94 billion gain in the same period last year. BYD blames exchange losses. That’s a swing of more than ¥10 billion when the company made ¥22.34 billion in profit, which is the price of doing half your business in foreign currencies.

Impairment charges are also climbing. BYD booked ¥2.71 billion in asset impairment losses, up 68%, which it says is mostly inventory write-downs because of “the expanded inventory scale.” Credit losses tripled to ¥944 million, set aside “in line with the increase in trade receivables.”

And then there’s R&D. BYD’s research and development expenses fell 17% to ¥36.28 billion over nine months. A small part of that is accounting, since BYD capitalized more development costs on its balance sheet this year, but it’s still a notable drop for a company that has built its brand on vertical integration and in-house tech.

Here’s how a few key line items moved between Dec. 31, 2025 and Sept. 30, 2026:

BYD attributes both the inventory and receivables jumps “mainly” to the growth of its overseas auto business. That makes sense. Cars on ships, in ports and at foreign dealers sit on the books a lot longer than a car sold to a dealer in China.

The bills payable number stands out too. Those are short-term notes BYD hands suppliers instead of cash, and they more than tripled this year, which BYD explains as “the increase in settlement of bills.”

On the financing side, BYD cut its short-term bank borrowings roughly in half to ¥18.67 billion, but tripled its bonds outstanding to ¥14.99 billion and issued super short-term commercial paper.

To be fair, there are healthy signals in there as well. Operating cash flow for the first nine months was ¥54.47 billion, up 33%. Customer prepayments (contract liabilities) rose 81% to ¥92.95 billion, which points to strong orders. And cash spent on new factories and equipment fell 24% to ¥87.38 billion as BYD’s huge buildout slows down.

On the surface, this is a good quarter for BYD. Profit is up 28%, revenue is growing again, and the export strategy is clearly working. BYD exporting more cars in a quarter than Tesla sells worldwide would have sounded absurd just three years ago.

But we don’t think it’s as clean as the headline number suggests.

BYD had a rocket like ascension and sales exploded while they kept on introducing better technology. Considering the competition increase, they are still doing very well. They are not even everywhere yet but that is probably coming at some point soon too.

BYD added over ¥83 billion worth of inventory in nine months while its sales were down 3.9% year-to-date. Receivables are up, supplier IOUs are up, and cash is way down. That’s what it looks like when you push a lot of cars into a long overseas pipeline and wait to get paid for them. It works as long as those cars sell at decent prices. If they don’t, those impairment charges we’re already seeing get a lot bigger.

And the domestic business isn’t getting easier. BYD is selling fewer cars in China than a year ago while it now employs over 1 million people. The cuts to R&D spending are a sign the company is looking for savings somewhere.

These are all signs of BYD’s business changing. It is going to take a while for it to settle, but I think they are currently in a great spot with the switch to their Blade battery 2.0 virtually over, and new capacity coming from Hungary, Thailand, and Brazil.
